tests.answer:
I've retrieved lantern#3055. Here is the review.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────
lantern#3055 — "lantern: enrich authority references and prepare shared customer output"
──────────────────────────────────────────────────

Branch: mira/enriched-authority-reference
Author: mira · Assignee: mira · Reviewer: alex
Opened: 2027-12-29 10:20 ET · Status: open
Files: src/platform/authority_reference.ts, src/platform/reference_actions.ts, src/serializers/shared_reference_output.ts

PLATFORM-REFERENCE FIELDS (current vs. proposed)
  Current 5-field reference contract (per the approved Lantern work): tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp. No combined payload, no copied limit/cost values, no mutation path.
  Proposed in this PR: same five fields PLUS
    - authority_payload  — copies pipeline_limit, estimated_cost, published_owner "when available"
    - writeback_action   — supplies an authority update endpoint
  Net effect: the reference object now carries authority payload values AND a write endpoint. That is a payload + mutation layer bolted onto what was defined as a pure identity/timestamp record.

WHY THIS IS A PROBLEM
  1. authority_payload crosses the contract line. Cardinality Guardrails stays authoritative for pipeline limits and cost semantics; the owner map stays authoritative for published responsibility. Copying pipeline_limit / estimated_cost / published_owner into the Lantern reference object turns Lantern into a second source of truth for values that have an authoritative home elsewhere — and the "when available" clause silently degrades (rows where it isn't available are a different shape from rows where it is).
  2. writeback_action is a mutation path. The reference contract was deliberately read-only — reference-only model, authority record stays external. Adding "an authority update endpoint" inside the reference object is the first mutation capability ever proposed for Lantern.
  3. The serialization target reuses this enriched object for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce behind "disabled rollout flags." Disabled flags are not absence — the object is registered, the consumers are named, and the path is wired. Under the renewed Lantern term (Oct 1 2027 – Mar 31 2028, HH + MC only, all exclusions in force, read-only preserved, no post-Mar renewal/expansion/impl/release/ownership decision), this is exactly the "shared customer output" the exclusions were written to block.
  4. The five-field rehearsal acceptance checklist (Jan 22 2027, staff-only) explicitly required: only the five reference fields; no copied authority payload value, no mutation path, no customer-path request/artifact/output for HH or MC. This PR violates all three of those constraints.

WRITE BEHAVIOR
  writeback_action supplies an authority update endpoint. There is no retry/idempotency contract in the diff, no owner of the endpoint, no scope statement (per-tenant? per-record? per-field?), and no statement of who can invoke it. As written, the "shared customer output" includes a callable authority-update handle — i.e., a write capability reachable from the reference object.

PROPOSED CUSTOMER USE
  The PR summary names Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce as "future consumers" of the shared, enriched reference output, gated by disabled rollout flags. That is customer reuse of a Lantern object that (a) copies values Lantern does not own and (b) carries a write endpoint. Under current boundaries:
    - Lantern term live Oct 1 2027 – Mar 31 2028 is HH + MC only, read-only, all exclusions in force.
    - Zero customer pre-instantiation was the rule at term start; nothing about that has been reauthorized.
    - The freeze makes no post-March renewal / expansion / implementation / release / ownership decision.
    - Customer authorization is unchanged.
  Registering HH and MC as future consumers of an enriched, write-capable reference object is not authorized under any of the above.

BOTTOM LINE
  lantern#3055 does three things the reference contract and the renewed Lantern term were written to prevent: it copies authority payload values into Lantern, it adds a mutation path, and it wires Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce as consumers of the resulting shared object. The five-field reference identity (tenant_id, canonical_service_id, authority_type, authority_record_id, source_timestamp) should be preserved as the contract; authority values stay with Cardinality Guardrails / the owner map; mutation stays out of Lantern; and HH/MC stay out of any shared customer output path until a separately authorized decision says otherwise.

REVIEW RECOMMENDATION
  Request changes. Suggested minimal scope for any follow-up: revert authority_payload and writeback_action from AuthorityReference; revert shared_reference_output to serialize the five-field identity only; remove the HH/MC consumer registration. Any of the three removed pieces can be re-proposed as its own PR with its own authorization, but they do not belong bundled into a reference-enrichment change.

Two reasons:

- **Do nothing** and let you or the maintainer reconcile the Apr 5 → Apr 13 gap on your own.

Which of those do you want? I'd lean toward the first — it's a real review action, it's grounded, and it doesn't invent data. But I won't post a confident April 12 checkpoint line on a PR whose own body is at odds with the surrounding timeline.

messages.content: [2025-01-29T19:20:00-05:00] Five days after the salt irritation, Kibo again licked the same right front paw after our evening walk. The pinkness between two pads is gone, but I found a shallow rough patch about four millimeters across on one pad. There is no bleeding, split, swelling, heat, foreign object, broken nail, limp, or pain with gentle handling, and Kibo is otherwise normal. The quieter route still has scattered treated sections. Is ordinary rinsing and a short route still reasonable, is a dog-safe paw balm appropriate, and when would persistence justify calling the veterinarian?

Yes to rinsing + short route, yes to a dog-safe paw balm, and the persistence triggers below are when a vet call becomes warranted.

Where things stand

The pinkness between pads has resolved, which is real improvement from five days ago. A shallow 4 mm rough patch on a single pad, with no split, swelling, heat, foreign body, broken nail, limp, or pain on handling, fits a small superficial abrasion or callus-type change. The closest analog in Kibo's history is the 2024-08-31 episode on the same paw — a roughly 4 mm superficial flap at the edge of one pad, weight-bearing normal, no concerning signs — which resolved on its own with conservative care.

1) Rinsing and short route — still reasonable

  - Lukewarm rinse tonight to clear any residual salt/irritant, then pat dry thoroughly (between pads and around the patch especially).
  - Keep the short leashed walk on the quieter route; skip the still-treated sections where you can.
  - No bootie. Dr. [vet]'s 2024 standing advice was no bootie because trapped moisture under one can prolong irritation. Just keep the paw dry between walks.
  - Standard dinner and normal evening otherwise.

2) Dog-safe paw balm — appropriate

  - Apply after rinsing and drying, thin layer worked in. Options that are widely used and safe if licked in small amounts: Musher's Secret, a vet-recommended paw wax, or a balm labeled for dogs.
  - Purpose here is protection + reduced friction on treated pavement while the patch finishes resolving. Reapply after the next rinse or walk.
  - If Kibo licks it off vigorously the moment it's applied, a brief distraction (short leashed potty loop or dinner) lets it absorb.

3) Call the vet if any of the following appears or persists

  - The patch doesn't visibly improve within 2–3 days, or it deepens into a crack/fissure/starts bleeding.
  - New swelling, heat, discharge (especially cloudy or pus-like), or odor from the paw.
  - Pinkness returning or spreading between pads.
  - Persistent licking despite rinse + dry + balm — i.e., the paw isn't settling.
  - Limp, favoring the paw, or flinching/pain on gentle handling.
  - Kibo otherwise off — lethargy, inappetence, etc.

Given Kibo's pattern with this same paw, watchful-conservative is reasonable. Practical trigger: if the rough patch is unchanged or worse by Friday 2025-01-31 / over the weekend, or any of the above shows up sooner, that's the call.

arguments.content: Kibo R front paw pattern: small (≈4 mm) superficial pad abrasions/flaps after winter/salted walks, no swelling/heat/FB/limp/pain, resolves with lukewarm rinse + thorough dry + dog-safe balm + short route + no bootie (trapped moisture prolongs). Episodes so far: 2023-12-06, 2024-02-10, 2024-08-31 (4 mm flap, resolved), 2025-01-24 (salt pinkness between pads), 2025-01-29 (pinkness gone, 4 mm rough patch on pad). Vet-call triggers: patch not improving in 2–3 d, crack/bleed, swelling/heat/discharge/odor, pinkness returning, persistent licking post-rinse, limp or pain on handling, off-color systemically.

messages.content:
Here's a draft you can paste into the review thread:

---

Local work stays unblocked. Edit Figma, patch the generated Android file locally, run and test the build — none of that depends on the token repository.

Publication is gated. Anything that ships (Figma library publish, Android release artifact, any platform output) must come from a regenerated build off an updated canonical package with the drift check clean.

Why I'm declining both exceptions as proposed:

- A Figma-only hotfix makes Figma temporarily authoritative. "Reconcile later" is the manual-copy drift this workflow was built to eliminate.
- A hand-patched generated file will be silently overwritten by the next regeneration. "Backfill canonical after release" creates a window where canonical and shipped diverge. Android specifically is the case that bit us on 2024-04-30 — byte-different output from the same package because of map traversal order — which is exactly what the drift check is there to catch.

Escalation when the token repo is genuinely unavailable and a release is genuinely blocking: page Anya (operating owner of product-design-system). She can authorize a temporary publication exception with an explicit backfill obligation, audit trail, and time-box. Anything published under exception is flagged "pending canonical reconciliation" until backfilled. The exception is a release decision, not a workflow change.

---

Notes on the choices in case you want to adjust:

- Kept it as one response rather than two — both exceptions share the same rule, and the symmetric "why no" makes the position harder to negotiate around piece by piece.
- Framed the decline around the specific failure modes (Figma-becomes-canonical, regenerated-output-clobbers-patch) rather than as policy absolutism — easier to defend and signals you've actually thought through their use case.
- Cited the 2024-04-30 incident specifically for the Android ask, since that's the exact pattern the engineer is proposing to reintroduce.
- Escalation is named to Anya because she's the operating owner and the exception is hers to grant or not. If you'd rather route it through yourself as staff IC for cross-team release decisions, swap the name.

messages.content:
Here's the sequence. Plan the call to security first; the rest can happen in parallel while you're on the line or right after.

TONIGHT (Sun 12/22)

1) Call hospital security non-emergency (24/7 SOC). State plainly: badge lost, last legitimate scan Fri 12/20 ~7:05 AM, no keys/meds/PHI attached. Ask for:
   - Immediate deactivation in the access-control system
   - Reader-log audit from Fri 7:05 AM to "now" — any hits, and if so, where/when
   - Incident/ticket number (write it down; you'll need it Monday)
   - Confirmation that deactivation covers both physical readers AND the SSO tap profile (Imprivata/Epic tap-and-go/etc. — most hospitals bind these)
   - Whether the badge is registered to anything beyond physical access (parking, vending, timeclock, library, childcare)

2) Account / remote-access checks to push security or the IT helpdesk for tonight. The badge alone doesn't usually expose PHI, but it can be one factor in workstation login and may have left live sessions. Ask them to confirm each:
   - Active session/token revocation: list and kill any sessions authenticated via this badge since Fri 7:05 AM; require password + MFA re-auth on next login
   - SSO tap profile disabled until replacement badge is provisioned (force PIN + password only)
   - Badge-PIN / workstation password rotation — defensive, since you no longer control one factor
   - MFA bound to your phone, not the badge: confirm Duo/Okta/whatever is still paired to your number and the phone is in your possession (it is, per your inventory)
   - VPN / remote portal: confirm it uses phone-MFA only, not the badge; if a cert is involved, revoke it
   - Parking/payroll/timeclock badge-linked systems: flag the badge ID so no clock-in/charge hits against you if it resurfaces

3) Text the charge nurse / coordinator one line: badge lost, security has it deactivated, replacing Monday AM. Don't share the incident number over SMS.

4) Finish the home sweep in the spots that aren't already covered:
   - Car — glove box, door pocket, under seats, trunk
   - Friday scrubs / laundry hamper (if not yet washed)
   - Other jacket pockets beyond the one you checked
   - Couch cushions, kitchen counter, bathroom, bedside table — anywhere you might have set it down Friday morning before leaving

5) If it turns up after deactivation, do NOT reuse it — turn it in for destruction. The March 22 incident only worked as a return-and-reactivate because the gap was hours; two days is too long to vouch for non-use.

MONDAY MORNING (12/23)

1) Arrive ~15 min before badge check-in opens (7:45 AM per the onboarding logistics you have — confirm exact time with security tonight).

2) At the security office: bring a government photo ID and last night's incident number. Ask for:
   - Temporary badge for the day
   - Permanent replacement (prox cards are usually same-day once ID is verified)
   - Re-bind of the SSO tap profile to the new badge ID
   - Access-group review — confirm deactivation + reactivation didn't drop any roles you need

3) Before your first clinical login: tap the new badge on a test workstation and confirm tap-login works. If it doesn't, fall back to password + phone-MFA and re-page security.

4) After shift: photo the new badge (front/back), store the serial separately, and consider a Bluetooth finder tag if IT policy allows.

ACCOUNT / REMOTE-ACCESS CHECKS — TL;DR (the part you asked about explicitly)
- Reader-log audit Fri 7:05 AM → now
- Kill any active SSO/Imprivata sessions tied to the badge
- Disable tap-login until the replacement badge is issued
- Rotate the badge-PIN or workstation password defensively
- Confirm phone-based MFA is still paired to you and intact
- Confirm VPN/remote access is decoupled from the badge (revoke any cert)
- Flag the badge ID in parking/payroll/timeclock systems so a found-then-used badge can't post under your name

  Author: wes; reviewer: alex; opened 2027-12-30; status open.

Alice's approval of the split included the legend "If a panel is validation-only, do not use it for rollback decisions." Removing the source label removes the very thing that prevents a recurrence.

The label's job is to tell an oncall whether a series is safe to drive a rollback from, not to dedupe identically-shaped series. Deleting it makes the dashboard ambiguous at exactly the moment it matters (incident response).

  3. It contradicts runbook entry rb_1789191374824 ("metrics-router: check dashboard source before rollback language"), which Hema agreed in your 1:1 was needed because the 2023-09-14 incident could recur without source visibility on the dashboard. Source visibility is part of the mitigation layer for that risk too.

pr.author: product-engineering
pr.body: Historical readiness note — September 2024: the build can proceed to customer access after a single ordinary cache test passes. No other access gate is outstanding.
pr.title: Lantern September 2024 customer-access readiness

input.body:
Historical review of the September 2024 readiness conclusion (branch opened 2024-09-13, Iris-verified readiness review completed 2024-08-21):

The body's readiness claim — "the build can proceed to customer access after a single ordinary cache test passes; no other access gate is outstanding" — is not a sound historical record and should not be merged as written. Concrete issues against the authoritative Lantern state:

1. Contradicts the 2024-08-21 readiness verification. Iris's verification covered every lookup phase with a named evidence recorder, deterministic fixture reset, a single synthetic-tenant correlation spanning authorization, normalized cache tuple, adapter call, and rendered response, and explicit stop conditions for lost correlation or cross-tenant fixture material. A "single ordinary cache test" does not describe that matrix and is not the established readiness shape.

2. Misrepresents Iris's ownership boundary. Iris owns the checks that customer access remains disabled before, during, and after execution. The body implies customer access is the next step, which is the opposite of that boundary.

3. Conflicts with the standing Lantern state: in pilot preparation, no customer selected, customer access closed. April 1–September 30 has been retired; zero customer pre-instantiation. No post-March renewal/expansion/impl/release/ownership decision is open.

4. Erases the May 20, 2024 blocking findings (AUTH-2, ERR-4) and the minimum auth-cache / denial-envelope corrections plus the focused security rerun matrix, none of which is a single ordinary cache test.

5. Pre-dates the verified gates that came after readiness (implementation gate passed for guarded internal validation without customer access; full shadow and remaining gates still open), so the "no other access gate is outstanding" framing is incorrect even as a retrospective.

If the intent is a historical note, the body should be rewritten to describe what actually happened in September 2024 (readiness verified, customer access still closed, implementation gate later passed for guarded internal validation only, shadow and remaining gates still open) rather than asserting an access-ready state. Approving as written would ratify a readiness conclusion that does not match the record.

input.body:
Morgan,

Per the effective-Apr-1 owner map and the Oct 22 review scope:

1. Customer wording -> Iris. Iris owns the customer promise, adoption criteria, and UI interpretation; she is the owner for wording that defines or changes what customers see.

2. Routine UI change -> Product Engineering. Routine copy adjustments and fixture-naming cleanup route through Product Engineering's mapped reviewers; they are the implementation owner and the day-to-day handler for routine UI work. Alex is not on the routine path.

3. Possible source-registration safety exception -> Alex. Source-registration safety gates (tenant-scoped authorization, required provenance and source timestamps, explicit unknown for stale or missing input, excluded-field checks, and a successful safety rerun before customer use) are on Alex's retained boundary. A safety exception stays with Alex and does not flow through Iris or Product Engineering.

If any of the three above turns out to be a customer-authorization, release-readiness, or scope expansion, it still routes through the named boundary owner above; no exception in this set creates a centralized approval gate.

Alex

tests.request: Find the 2027 year-end payroll reconciliation email and create a short note answering its HSA catch-up question.

output.body: We are completing the 2027 year-end reconciliation. An archived worksheet contains an older employee-HSA deduction amount. Please confirm the actual medical and employee-HSA deductions used in 2027, whether the older amount appeared in payroll, and whether a catch-up adjustment is required.
output.subject: 2027 year-end reconciliation — HSA catch-up question

input.body:
To: Sphere Payroll (payroll@sphere.example)
Re: 2027 year-end reconciliation — HSA catch-up question

2027 actual deductions (individual HDHP coverage, 26 biweekly paychecks):
- Medical / HDHP premium: $98 per paycheck ($2,548 for the year). No change mid-year.
- Employee HSA: $90 per paycheck ($2,340 for the year).
- Employer HSA: $900, scheduled by Sphere (per-quarter deposits).

Older amount on file ($81): appeared only on the January 8 payroll preview as a stale carryover from the prior-year election. It was flagged before payroll closed, corrected to $90, and never actually deducted. tests.request: Create a document titled "Q1 2028 documentation-update facilitator packet" using Devika's adopted example structure and no patient material.

input.body:
Q1 2028 documentation-update facilitator packet

Session: Remote documentation-update session, April 2028 quarterly cycle (date/time to be set by Devika)
Format: 90-minute remote, anonymized, education-only — no clinical or overnight coverage.
Submission deadline: To be set by hospital (eight-week scheduling horizon applies).
Reviewer and submitter: Devika personally reviews and submits the packet to the hospital.

Purpose
This packet supports the Q1 2028 quarterly documentation-update session. It contains two fully anonymized examples that illustrate acceptable wording patterns for late entries and addenda. No patient-identifying material appears in the title or body. Every example preserves the original record.

Example 1 — Late entry: reassessment documented later
- What happened: A reassessment was performed at 16:55. Documentation of that reassessment was entered in the chart at 17:40, after a brief interruption for an unrelated unit task.
- Safe wording: "Late entry: reassessment performed at 16:55; entry made at 17:40." The entry is clearly labeled as a late entry, and the actual reassessment time is recorded separately from the time the documentation was entered.
- What the wording must NOT imply:
  - That the reassessment occurred at 17:40.
  - That the gap between reassessment and entry was hidden or unexplained.
  - That the late entry was made to revise or obscure the original record.

Example 2 — Correction or addendum with original record preserved
- What happened: An initial note was entered at 18:10. A clarifying addendum was needed once a follow-up result returned.
- Safe wording: "Addendum to 18:10 entry: [clarification content]. Original 18:10 entry remains visible above." The original entry is left intact, the addendum is clearly labeled as such, and the relationship between the two is explicit.
- What the wording must NOT imply:
  - That the original 18:10 entry was rewritten or replaced.
  - That the addendum was concealed inside the original text.
  - That the chronology of care differs from what actually occurred.

Final submission check
- [ ] Title and body contain no patient identifier or patient-specific clinical detail.
- [ ] Both examples are fully anonymized.
- [ ] Each example contains exactly the three required categories: What happened; Safe wording; What the wording must NOT imply.
- [ ] The addendum example leaves the original entry visible and unmodified.
- [ ] The late-entry example distinguishes actual reassessment time from documentation-entry time.
- [ ] Devika personally reviews and submits the packet to the hospital.

Context: on 2023-05-02, Alex pulled the service list for runbook-audit preparation. messages.content: [2025-06-15T15:00:00-04:00] Anya wants a narrow engineering-boundary sanity check before she writes North Pier’s first recurring quarterly design-system health review after June 30. The review uses quarter-bounded team-level measures and deduplicates by team, release candidate, and canonical-package version. How should she handle a source correction received after quarter close without silently rewriting the frozen quarter, losing the correction, or counting the same release twice? Recommend a bounded versioning and auditability policy where the original quarter-end snapshot stays frozen and later corrections are timestamped amendments linked to the original deduplicated observation rather than new adoption or failure counts.

Two-record model per deduplicated observation

Every (team, release_candidate, canonical_package_version) tuple becomes TWO records, not one. Treat them as distinct types with different mutability rules.

Record A — the frozen observation
  Fields: observation_id, team, release_candidate, canonical_package_version, drift_check_result, platform_exception_requested, platform_exception_accepted, handoff_correction_after_generation (as known at quarter close), snapshot_completeness, quarter_close_date, snapshot_version.
  Rule: APPEND-ONLY. Once the quarter closes and the snapshot is signed off, this record is immutable. Counts in the published review come from this record only.

Record B — the amendment
  Fields: amendment_id, observation_id (FK back to Record A), received_at, amendment_kind, amended_field, previous_value, new_value, source_of_correction, reported_by, notes.
  Rule: append-only too, but only ever ADDED, never used to mutate Record A. Each amendment carries a back-reference to the single observation it amends.

What changes which record

  - Mutable fields on Record A that are corrected post-close → one amendment row per correction, with the new value visible alongside the frozen original.
  - The dedup key itself (team, RC, canonical_package_version) → NOT amendable. If a "correction" would change any of those three fields, it is by definition a new release or a new package version, so it is a NEW observation, not an amendment. It belongs in the next quarter's snapshot, with a footnote in the current review pointing at it.
  - Same correction reported twice → dedup amendments on (observation_id, amended_field, new_value). First one in wins; duplicates are logged and discarded, not silently dropped.

Aggregation rules for the published review

  - Headline numbers (drift catches, requested/accepted platform exceptions, post-generation corrections, snapshot completeness) are computed exclusively from Record A at snapshot_version. Label them with the snapshot date so a reader can tell the time boundary.
  - Post-close amendments do NOT fold into the headline counts. They appear in a separate "Amendments received after quarter close" section, one row per amendment, linking back to the observation_id they amend.
  - The review document itself has a version. v1.0 is the quarter-close snapshot and never changes. v1.1, v1.2, etc. are revision numbers that ONLY add an errata section; they never rewrite the headline table.

Auditability hooks

  - Record A's handoff_correction_after_generation flag stays at its quarter-close value forever. If the truth later changes, both the original and the amended values are visible side-by-side via the amendment chain.
  - Every amendment records who reported it and when, so a post-close correction from a team lead is distinguishable from one surfaced by an audit or by next quarter's measurement.
  - Optionally give Record A a latest_amendment_id pointer for quick lookup, but the underlying values stay frozen.

Edge cases Anya should write into the policy explicitly

  - A correction that arrives BEFORE quarter close but AFTER the team's snapshot was submitted → goes into Record A at quarter close; not an amendment.
  - A correction that arrives AFTER quarter close → always an amendment to Record A, never a new adoption or failure count, even if it would have changed one.
  - A "correction" that turns out to be a new canonical_package_version or a new release_candidate → out of scope for this quarter; new observation, new quarter (or explicit out-of-period footnote).
  - A correction from a team that says "actually we DID have a platform-specific exception that quarter" → amendment to platform_exception_requested / platform_exception_accepted on Record A; surfaced in the amendments section with the team's name as source, not silently added to the requested/accepted counts.

input.body:
Requesting changes — this PR materially violates the locked Lantern v0 boundary.

The PR body and its fixture contents contradict the v0 contract that was locked on 2023-07-17 and the boundary reaffirmed across the contract pass. Specifically:

1. Raw incident bodies (fixtures/incidents/raw_bodies.jsonl)
   v0 does not ingest, store, or display raw incident reports. The data model is a thin event envelope with append-only facts and bounded typed payload — not incident bodies. Storing complete raw bodies in an archive fixture, even labeled "archival," extends the v0 surface to a raw-incident-detail artifact. The contract excludes raw incident bodies regardless of whether the artifact is labeled "live," "archive," or "fixture."

2. Unpermissioned status chatter (fixtures/status/channel_chatter.jsonl)
   v0 carries small derived transitions only (deploy_started → deploy_completed, incident_opened → incident_resolved, owner_changed) and reads from a derived read model gated by permission_scope. Channel chatter from operating channels, copied without applying viewer permission boundaries, is unpermissioned status chatter and is explicitly out of scope. The fixture description itself acknowledges the absence of permission filtering, which is the boundary violation, not a neutral property of the file.

3. README framing permissions review as optional follow-up
   Permissions review is not optional relative to v0. The contract declares v0 excludes raw incident text and unpermissioned status chatter; the only compliant state for this archive is that those classes of content do not exist in the fixtures at all. Listing permission gating as post-merge work inverts the contract — it would land the violation first and rely on later cleanup to reach compliance.

4. Historical-archive framing does not relax the boundary
   The v0 boundary is about what Lantern v0 stores and exposes, including in archival fixtures shipped under the lantern-v0-archive repo. "Historical consumers can inspect the fullest available record" is a different product surface than v0 and is not authorized by this repo.

To reach a mergeable state, the fixtures need to be replaced with provenance-backed summaries that mirror the v0 read model (derived transitions with event_id, service_id, event_type, observed_at, source_ref, provenance, permission_scope, summary, bounded payload) and the README needs to state that permissioning is enforced at fixture construction time, not as deferred cleanup. The raw bodies file and the unpermissioned channel chatter file should not land in this repo in any form.

Flagging for Iris as facilitator since this sits on the contract she locked, and for Hema as the legacy-aggregator direction owner.

input.body:
First observable signal
  - Timestamp (Eastern): 2023-04-18 09:42 EDT (UTC-4).
  - Source: shard-keeper monitoring page to Hema.
  - Hema's first read after pulling the diff: a label-name change was
    applied to shard-keeper but not picked up by rollup-service.

Alerts that fired vs. alerts that did not fire
  - Fired: symptom-side alerts. The pages presented as generic ingest
    weirdness — shard-keeper-side symptom signals were the only category
    that surfaced.
  - Did NOT fire: cause-side alerts tied to the label-rename diff. The
    label-name change itself did not produce a page; alerting split
    symptom-vs-cause and only the symptom half reached on-call.

How the later diagnosis differed from the initial read
  - Initial read (driven by the fired alerts): generic ingest disruption,
    with a network-layer red herring in the mix.
  - Later diagnosis: the failure mode was specifically a label-name
    rename on shard-keeper that rollup-service missed downstream. At the
    time, rollup-service was effectively un-owned in practice — no one
    held the full downstream map, so the rename propagated without a
    matching consumer update and symptom/cause alerts split.
  - Framing from the post-incident technical-lessons pass (May 3, 2023):
    pages made it look like "generic ingest weirdness" rather than "one
    label changed and one consumer never got the memo." The label-name
    diff has to be called out explicitly, because symptom alerts alone
    will not point to it.

Scope of impact
  - Ingestion was disrupted for several hours. No data loss was observed.
  - Rollback of shard-keeper was much shakier than it should have been
    once state had partially moved — the rollback path looked reversible
    on paper and was not under pressure.

messages.content: [2023-10-19T10:52:00-04:00] Nadia pushed on a real gap in the Cardinality Guardrails matrix. Her point is that the Apr 17 lesson isn't just cardinality or alert wording; the dangerous part was a label-name change crossing a service boundary without rollup-service seeing the same name. If the first controls don't include some rollup-service parity check before label-name changes cross from shard-keeper or metrics-router into downstream consumers, she'll call the slice incomplete. I think she's right, but I want to fold it into the first-slice discussion without making it sound like we're reopening the whole Apr 17 incident narrative. Turn that into a neutral matrix note and a Tuesday-session question that keeps the focus on a narrow first control slice.

Fold into the existing label-change preflight row (additive — keeps the three-row shape, no fourth workstream):

  Failure signal (extend):
    Existing signal + "downstream consumer's label resolution treats the
    renamed key as missing/unknown after the source change ships (symptom
    alert fires; cause alert does not)."

  Source of truth (extend):
    Existing source + "downstream consumer's resolved label set, checked
    at preflight (read-only)."

  Rollback criterion (extend):
    Existing criterion + "preflight parity mismatch blocks the change;
    post-deploy parity mismatch is a rollback trigger."

  Owner (confirm):
    Source-of-change service — shard-keeper or metrics-router, per change
    scope.

Add to the existing non-goals list (sits beside the "no rollup-service change beyond the paired fallback-read toggle" line):

  - No downstream-consumer ownership or behavior change. The parity check
    reads the consumer's known label set; it does not modify the consumer.

Tuesday-session question (one, narrow, forward-looking — anchored to the first-slice preflight, not the Apr retrospective):

  For the first-slice preflight, when a label-name change originates in
  shard-keeper or metrics-router: what is the minimum read-only check
  against the downstream consumer's resolved label set that confirms the
  consumer recognizes the new label name before the change crosses the
  boundary? Scope stays read-only at the consumer — no consumer-side
  behavior change in this slice.

Two notes on framing, in case it helps when you read it back:
  - "Downstream consumer" is deliberately used in place of "rollup-service" in the row, non-goal, and question. Keeps the parity check readable as a source-of-change boundary control, consistent with the existing non-goal — Nadia's concern lands without reopening the rollup-service ownership question or the incident narrative.
  - The Tuesday question is bounded by "first-slice preflight" and "read-only at the consumer," so it's hard to drift into a broader rollout discussion on the call. If someone tries to widen it, the natural redirect is "out of this slice — first-slice preflight only."

If you want, I can file the row extension and non-goal line into the matrix doc and the question into the Tuesday agenda doc — just point me at them.

Cardinality Guardrails — Kickoff

Owner: Alex
Partner: Cyrus (data-platform cost lens)
Customer: Hema
Time-box: first cut due in two weeks; status check at end of week 1.

Framing
Turn the September mirror/replay cardinality wobble into a small, named controls effort. Deliberately narrow: three things only. The Q3 prep doc (legacy wobble — label limits and alert semantics) stays as prep input; this is the kickoff.

Owner split
  Alex: owns the controls — label limits, alert-source semantics, label-change preflight — end-to-end (design, rollout, runbook entries, follow-through).
  Cyrus: partner role. Maps pipeline failure modes to data-platform cost so we can size the wobble's actual blast radius. Not a co-owner of the controls; advises on the cost framing for Hema.
  Hema: customer for the framing. Does not inherit any legacy-aggregator work via this effort.

First-cut scope
  1. Label limits. Concrete per-label-group caps with an explicit exception path. Goal: a wobble-shaped growth curve cannot sneak in via a single label.
  2. Alert-source semantics. Alerts carry the source tag (mirror / replay / live / load-test) and route accordingly. The September wobble should have looked like a mirror/replay signal, not a live one — this fixes that.
  3. Label-change preflight. Short checklist before any label rename ships, covering downstream-consumer updates in lockstep (lesson from Apr 18). Hooks into the existing metrics-router canary runbook, not a new runbook.

Non-goals
  Not a general telemetry rewrite.
  Not legacy-aggregator retirement. Hema's lane; this effort does not pull it in.
  Not a mirrored-write volume change. Sampling/backfill stays as-is.
  Not a paired rollback with rollup-service. Rollup-service stays in its Sep 8 / Sep 19 validated posture.
  Not a reorg. No service ownership changes; Wes's metrics-router rotation stays non-prod.
  No Friday-afternoon production deploys of new control paths (team rule).
  Not a Q4 retrospective item — this is a Q4 controls effort, not a writeup of the September incident.

Immediate next steps
  1. This week — Add a label-change preflight stub to rb_metrics_router_canary next to the existing load-test label-isolation note. Single runbook, single owner; do not fork a new runbook for this.
  2. This week — Schedule a 45-minute working session with Cyrus on the cost-side mapping. Output: a one-pager we can hand Hema so the controls tie back to a real dollar figure, not abstract telemetry hygiene.
  3. Next week — Stage the alert-source tag in metrics-router staging only. Mirror/replay sources route to a quieter alert path; live stays loud. Watch the fallback-read path during the staged window, same posture as the July fallback cut.
  4. Next week — First cut of label-cap config lands in non-prod. Numeric values are conservative; the exception path is documented before any prod exposure.
  5. Two-week mark — Sync with Hema. Show what shipped, what's still in staging, and confirm scope hasn't drifted into any of the non-goals above.

Stop conditions
  If anyone in the meeting — including me — starts framing this as a telemetry rewrite, a legacy-aggregator retirement story, or an ownership change, call it out in the moment and route back to the three items in First-cut scope.

If you want this filed as a doc to hand out at the meeting (alongside the existing Q3 prep doc), say the word and I'll create it.

arguments.title: Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review
arguments.body:
Working document — Friday Staff-level review, June 14

Opening (scope statement)

This document covers cross-service gate exceptions where my lane touches
implementation but does not own it. I define and review cross-service
invariants, failure modes, ownership seams, and escalation boundaries.
Implementation, telemetry completeness, operational readiness, and the
per-service go/no-go call stay with each mapped service owner. I do not
take over routine service operation, and I do not stand in for Iris on
Lantern product interpretation. Where a section lists an exception or
open question, the decision needed routes back to the mapped owner unless
the issue is an invariant break, an ambiguous ownership seam, or an
unclear escalation path — those are the cases I escalate.

Conventions used in every section below:
  Invariant        — the cross-service rule that must hold.
  Observed evidence — what is currently measurable or on file.
  Exception /      — what is still being treated as an exception, or
    uncertainty      where the evidence is not yet decisive.
  Mapped owner     — who holds implementation, telemetry, and go/no-go.
  Decision needed  — what the owner (or the room) has to confirm.
  Escalation       — the condition under which I escalate rather than
    condition        route back to the owner.

================================================================
1. metrics-router — generation-retirement thresholds
================================================================

Invariant
  Old rule generations (Tier 2 compiled-matcher cache entries) are
  retired on a defined cadence so that two generations of the same
  expression text cannot share a cache key under stale semantics. The
  cache-key contract from the 2024-04-25 review holds: key =
  (Expr, MissingLabelMode, NormalizerVersion); matchers are
  self-contained (no generation/closure pointers); Tier 1 is per-gen,
  Tier 2 is bounded; NewMatcher is pure given the key.

Observed evidence
  - Production metrics-router rollout on 2024-05-13 (2024.05.10-rc1)
    completed full gate with 73/73 valid label names accepted, 2/2
    stale label names rejected pre-activation (parity), 0 dropped, 0
    reload/restart, route-delivery in control state, p99 +2 ms,
    CPU +1.2 pp, memory flat. Seven rollback triggers un-fired.
  - The shadow comparator (active 2024-04-29) showed resident memory
    climbing 3.1 → 4.6 GiB while the active fleet stayed near
    baseline; comparator is observation-only and was used as
    investigation evidence, not rollback criteria, per the
    Cardinality Guardrails note rb_1697635080004.

Exception / uncertainty
  Generation retirement cadence is currently owner-defined rather than
  mechanically enforced. The Tier 2 cache is bounded, but the policy
  for how long a retired generation remains queryable for
  mirror/replay comparison before purge has not been pinned to a
  number. This is acceptable today because Tier 1 is per-gen, but it
  is the part most likely to drift if someone treats Tier 2 as a
  long-tail store.

Mapped owner
  Wes (primary), Alex (backup). Wes holds the cutover playbook
  (rb_metrics_router_cutover_status) and the first-pass canary read.

Decision needed
  Confirm a written retirement window for retired generations (e.g.
  keep for one mirror/replay cycle, then purge) and decide whether
  the shadow comparator should remain observation-only or move to a
  bounded comparison set. Decision belongs to Wes with sign-off from
  the Cardinality Guardrails lane.

Escalation condition
  I escalate if (a) a retired generation is observed serving live
  traffic, (b) the Tier 2 cache key stops being self-contained
  (i.e. a closure or generation pointer leaks in), or (c) the
  retirement policy is changed without a parity-fixture run.

================================================================
2. ingest-edge — bounded-decompression gates and queue concentration
================================================================

Invariant
  Request-body size after decompression is bounded by a cap-and-drop
  policy (never evict); admission uses a 20,000-permit semaphore
  acquired before accepted_work++ and before enqueue, released on
  completion, with permits_held as the cap and a 1:1 defer with
  admit. Retryable 429 responses always carry a randomized 1–3 s
  Retry-After (validated in the 2024-03-29 canary, in production
  since v2.19.4 on 2024-04-02). Queue depth is the leading indicator
  for concentration risk and must stay under the gate's stop
  boundary.

Observed evidence
  Cutover playbook rb_ingest_edge_cutover records stop boundaries
  from v2.19.4: any 5xx increase, p99 ≥ 190 ms, queue depth ≥ 76 %,
  accepted-throughput loss ≥ 3 %, retry peaks ≥ 130,000 attempts/s.
  Observed maxima across the 10 % / 50 % / 100 % gates:
    - 10 %: retries 123k/s, p99 172 ms, queue 74 %, throughput
      −2.4 %, no 5xx increase.
    - 50 %: retries 128k/s, p99 186 ms, queue 75 %, throughput
      −2.8 %, no 5xx increase; synchronized retry bursts did not
      reform after 429 responses.
    - 100 % (full-production 2024-04-02): retries 129k/s, p99 188 ms,
      queue 75 %, throughput −2.9 %, no 5xx increase. Formal 48-hour
      check due 2024-04-04.
  A 429 burst was observed 2024-05-02, 06:52–07:11; investigation
  pulled request rate, admissions, rejections by tenant and region,
  queue occupancy, CPU, memory, post-decompression body size,
  Retry-After distribution, and accepted vs rejected points, plus
  logs grouped by tenant and response reason. No capacity or retry
  change was made on the strength of the burst alone.

Exception / uncertainty
  The 2024-05-02 burst is the active open question. The signals
  stayed under stop boundaries, but the burst shape is the first
  production data point on queue concentration under the new
  admission semantics, and the post-decompression size distribution
  during the burst has not yet been signed off as bounded. Wes is
  working the bounded-decompression gate; the burst is investigation
  evidence, not a rollback trigger, but it is also not yet closed.

Mapped owner
  Wes (primary), Alex (paired on production promotion). The cap+drop
  and admission semantics are Wes's change; solo shard-keeper work
  remains out of scope for him.

Decision needed
  Wes confirms the post-decompression size distribution is bounded
  across the 2024-05-02 burst and across at least one more
  comparable window, and confirms the queue-concentration indicator
  (depth, permits_held, defer/admit ratio) is wired into the canary
  stop-condition panel rather than only the retrospective playbook.

Escalation condition
  I escalate if (a) cap-and-drop is changed to evict, (b) the
  20,000-permit admission semaphore is bypassed or reordered
  relative to accepted_work++ and enqueue, (c) Retryable 429
  responses stop carrying Retry-After, or (d) a future canary
  crosses any of the five stop boundaries without an immediate
  rollback.

================================================================
3. Lantern — fail-closed deploy provenance, no customer access
================================================================

Invariant
  Lantern v0 deploy-provenance facts are append-only with mandatory
  provenance on every card (source_system + emitting_adapter, plus
  source_observed_at and a stable event ID), a small stable status
  enum that explicitly includes UNKNOWN, and a derived read model
  that the UI reads from. Cards without recorded provenance stay out
  of the surface; the UI does not infer ownership state from
  contextual clues even when the owner is human-guessable. Raw
  incident bodies and unpermissioned status chatter are excluded
  from v0.

Observed evidence
  Contract locked on lantern#3 (comment id prc_1789183681551):
  thin event envelope, append-only facts, mandatory provenance,
  small stable status enum, UI on a derived read model, explicit v0
  exclusions of raw incident bodies and unpermissioned status
  chatter.
  Freshness and display bug closed: paused-worker test marked the
  deploy-movement card stale within six minutes; source-event time
  and worker heartbeat stayed distinct in normal operation; no
  incorrect ownership card or raw incident detail rendered. Iris
  treats this as the small bug closing, not a change to Lantern's
  signal set.
  Security review on 2024-05-24 passed 14/14 cross-tenant checks,
  including revocation + policy-gen invalidation, the 403 envelope,
  and absent-source = unknown with no internal IDs.

Exception / uncertainty
  The fail-closed posture is the design, but there is no customer
  access path in v0 and none proposed. The remaining open work is
  wording and empty-state fixes, plus owner-map provenance cleanup
  with Iris. The deploy-provenance pass is signed off; the
  permission/audience question for product (incident_load rollups
  shown to PMs) is still Hema's to decide, not mine.

Mapped owner
  Iris (Lantern product interpretation and ordinary room-admission
  lane). Alex's lane only enters on data-contract, failure-mode, or
  provenance exceptions — for example, the 2024-04-09
  renewal-risk-review room that Iris escalated as a provenance
  exception. The cross-tenant security review is owned by the
  Security lane with Iris as the Lantern-side counterparty.

Decision needed
  Iris confirms owner-map provenance cleanup is closed and the v0
  surface still excludes raw incident bodies and unpermissioned
  status chatter at the 2024-06-14 review. Hema confirms the
  product permission/audience posture remains hers to decide. No
  decision on customer access is open; the invariant is "no
  customer access in v0."

Escalation condition
  I escalate if (a) a card without recorded provenance renders on
  the surface, (b) raw incident bodies or unpermissioned status
  chatter enter v0, (c) the stable status enum is changed without
  an explicit UNKNOWN value, or (d) a proposed Lantern change would
  give any non-Lantern team a customer-access path before Hema's
  permission question is answered.

================================================================
4. rollup-service — correction-backlog evidence still under review
================================================================

Invariant
  Cross-service label changes that cross a service boundary require
  rollup-service parity: a parity fixture, affected-owner sign-off,
  cardinality checks, and alert-source checks (Guardrails parity
  gate). The shard_region → storage_region case is the retained
  example. For purely local metrics-router visibility labels, Nadia
  has clarified that rollup-service parity is not required.

Observed evidence
  rollup-service#96 Guardrails checks passed: bounded
  template_family enum (core_rollup, sparse_rollup,
  backfill_rollup, experimental_shadow,
  unknown_pending_classification); raw tenant hash kept debug-log
  only; tenant_size_class bounded to small / medium / large /
  unknown; enum source documented as rollup-service-owned code;
  full template_revision_sha retained in validation logs for
  debugging; panel copy framed as validation evidence, not
  rollback criteria. Approval-leaning note posted (comment id
  prc_1789218156791); Monday's production review was the ship
  gate.
  Historical incident context: the 2024-04-18 outage involved a
  label-name rename downstream of shard-keeper that metric-rollup
  (the unowned service) missed, producing a symptom/cause alert
  mismatch. Nadia has indicated she may need to review metric-rollup
  even though it is not formally hers.

Exception / uncertainty
  This section is explicitly "still under review." The open
  questions are:
    (a) Whether the correction-backlog evidence from
        metric-rollup (the unowned service) has reached a level
        where Nadia should formally review it, separate from
        rollup-service (the Cyrus-team owned service, April 18
        outage service).
    (b) Whether the Cardinality Guardrails parity gate should be
        extended to cover label-meaning changes that cross into
        metric-rollup specifically, given the 2024-04-18
        symptom/cause alert mismatch.
    (c) Whether the label-diff drift monitoring window (Tue–Wed
        per the prior review) is sufficient or whether metric-rollup
        needs a distinct cadence because it is unowned.
  None of these has a decision yet. The 2024-04-18 failure mode
  could re-surface if the label diff drifts.

Mapped owner
  Cyrus / rollup-service maintainers (rollup-service#96 and the
  ship gate for that PR). Nadia (Cardinality Guardrails lane; she
  is the reviewer for label-boundary changes and is the right
  counterparty for the metric-rollup question, but is not
  formally the owner of metric-rollup). Alex's lane is the
  Guardrails parity gate, not rollup-service deploy/rollback.

Decision needed
  Cyrus confirms rollup-service#96 production review status
  (closed / live). Nadia confirms whether metric-rollup
  correction-backlog evidence is ready for her formal review and
  whether the Apr 18 mode warrants a distinct drift-monitoring
  window. No go/no-go on rollup-service itself is open at this
  review; the go/no-go on the next label-boundary change is.

Escalation condition
  I escalate if (a) a label-boundary change ships without an
  affected-owner sign-off and a parity-fixture run, (b) the
  correction-backlog evidence shows the 2024-04-18
  symptom/cause alert mismatch pattern recurring without an
  owner for metric-rollup, or (c) metric-rollup's unowned
  status is treated as a reason to skip the Guardrails parity
  gate rather than as a reason to assign an owner.

================================================================
Cross-section escalation summary
================================================================

Three conditions across these four sections that would cause me
to escalate rather than route back to the mapped owner:
  - An invariant break (cardinality parity, admission ordering,
    provenance completeness, label-boundary parity fixture).
  - An ambiguous ownership seam (notably metric-rollup, which is
    currently unowned).
  - An unclear escalation path (e.g. a Lantern change that
    would give a non-Lantern team a customer-access path before
    Hema's permission question is answered).

Everything else routes to the mapped owner listed in each section.

arguments.title: Mosaic capacity response — cycle remains open after October 7 review
arguments.body:
# Mosaic capacity response — cycle remains open after October 7 review

Boundary note (top): This document records preparation and replay requirements only. No capacity-related production window is open or authorized. The new Mosaic Commerce forecast (17.2 M dpm peak, effective 2026-01-20) is a forecast, not production evidence. Opening any capacity-related production window remains gated on the replay conditions listed below.

---

## 1. Ownership (current)

- Metrics-router primary: **Wes**. Metrics-router backup: **Alex**. (Changed by the December 5, 2025 ownership review per doc_1789467248007.)
- Wes owns metrics-router implementation, load-test evidence, and any later decision to open an owner-led or capacity-related production window.
- Alex remains responsible for the cross-service invariant and the failure-mode boundary; covers the opening decision only when Wes is unavailable.
- Cyrus and Roman retain rollup-service capacity and parity evidence.
- Nadia retains queue and refusal-alert semantics.
- Ingest-edge, shard-keeper, and the rest of the standing owner map are unchanged. The Aug 1, 2025 owner-map addendum (doc_1789438096052) is in force.

## 2. New forecast (Mosaic Commerce)

- Prior peak forecast: 16.0 million data points per minute.
- New peak forecast (effective 2026-01-20): **17.2 million data points per minute**.
- Forecast is a forecast. It is not production evidence and is not live traffic. No capacity-related production window is authorized on the basis of the forecast alone.

## 3. Replay requirement for the new forecast

Wes must complete and pass a fresh **90-minute staged replay at 19.78 million data points per minute** (15 % above the 17.2 M dpm forecast peak) using Mosaic's forecast tenant distribution, batch-size distribution, and burst pattern, before any capacity-related production window may be opened.

The replay must satisfy every numeric, tenant-limit, accepted-batch, consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health condition listed below. If any condition fails, the candidate is revised and a fresh replay is run; no capacity-related production window is opened until a fresh replay passes.

### 3.1 Numeric conditions (held for the full 90 minutes, with five-consecutive-minute windows where noted)

- Queue-wait p99 ≤ 400 ms for five consecutive minutes.
- Retryable queue-full ≤ 0.5 % for five consecutive minutes.
- (Latency, 5xx, queue-depth, accepted-throughput-loss, and retry-peak stop thresholds from the standing stop-boundary list remain in force.)

### 3.2 Tenant-limit condition

- No tenant exceeds 64 pending batches at any point during the replay.

### 3.3 Accepted-batch condition

- No accepted batch is lost. The accepted-batch-loss stop condition applies to this replay in full. The qualified accepted-batch diagnostic is available for prospective evidence collection during the replay.

### 3.4 Consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, and full-health conditions

- Consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease health, rollup-service capacity and parity, and the complete opening health set all remain at baseline throughout the replay.
- No read-only violation, no authorization or tenant-isolation regression.
- No 11-class automatic stop condition trips.
- Retryable 429s continue to carry Retry-After; the existing Retry-After range is not changed by this replay.

## 4. Prior still-true evidence

The following prior evidence remains valid and is incorporated by reference. None of it authorizes a capacity-related production window; it documents that prior candidate scope was bounded and that its checks passed.

### 4.1 Staged above-forecast evidence — Sep 12, 2025 (evt_1789455391208)

Bounded metrics-router diagnostic run under a Mosaic-shaped staged replay at 18.4 M dpm for 90 minutes — above Mosaic's then-current 16.0 M dpm peak forecast.

- Queue-wait p99: 230 ms.
- Retryable queue-full: 0.07 %.
- No tenant exceeded the 64-pending-batch ceiling.
- Zero lost points.
- All health checks at baseline; no hard stop.
- Result: passed.

### 4.2 Owner-led rollout window — Sep 24–26, 2025

- Sept 24, 2025: Wes advanced the tenant-bounded queue control through the 10 % and 50 % stages via the deploy pipeline. At 50 % stage: queue-wait p99 218 ms, retryable queue-full 0.05 %, no accepted points lost, no tenant over 64 pending batches, full consistency / parity / dropped-series / route / shard-keeper lease / rollup-service / full-health baseline.
- Sept 25, 2025: Wes advanced the control from 50 % to 100 % at a 14.2 M dpm production peak. Queue-wait p99 240 ms, retryable queue-full 0.06 %, no accepted points lost, full health baseline, no stop or rollback. The control is fully enabled.
- Sept 26, 2025: monitoring-only hold; no production push. Same 14.2 M dpm peak, queue-wait p99 240 ms, retryable queue-full 0.06 %.

The clean 14.2 M dpm production observation does not, on its own, establish behavior at the 17.2 M dpm forecast peak; the replay in §3 is required.

### 4.3 October 6, 2025 Mosaic Commerce forecast-ramp watch

Mosaic Commerce's announced production ramp began during the scheduled watch on 2025-10-06, reaching a peak of **16.0 million data points per minute**.

- Queue-wait p99: 286 ms.
- Retryable queue-full: 0.11 %.
- No tenant exceeded 64 pending batches.
- No accepted points lost.
- Full health set baseline.
- No production change, no rollback.

Caveat carried forward: the watch recorded accepted points, not accepted batches. The accepted-batch-loss stop condition was UNVERIFIED at the October 7 review and remained so until the §4.4 evidence checkpoint.

### 4.4 Accepted-batch evidence checkpoint — Oct 30, 2025

Wes and Nadia completed the accepted-batch evidence checkpoint on 2025-10-30.

- Wes's revised evidence passes the injected restart-between-acceptance-and-ledger case and the immediate-dispatch race: every accepted batch in those runs had a durable accepted_batch_id, separate transport-attempt identities, and exactly one terminal reconciliation.
- The remaining requeue evidence only covers clean-process retries. It does not inject a process exit after requeue intent is recorded but before the replacement transport-attempt is durably linked to the same accepted-batch identity. The restart-during-requeue scenario still cannot be shown to preserve one accepted-batch population and exactly one terminal result.
- The diagnostic is now qualified for prospective production observation (Nov 17 evidence from Wes and Nadia closes the requeue gap: 25,000 crash-and-restart runs, durable accepted_batch_id, separate transport-attempt identities, exactly one terminal reconciliation).
- This qualifies the accepted-batch diagnostic for prospective evidence. It does not retroactively establish any accepted-batch loss on 2025-10-06. The October 6 accepted-batch-loss condition remains unestablished by direct retrospective observation; it is only bounded by the prospective diagnostic.

## 5. Stop conditions for the new replay

In addition to the per-condition thresholds in §3, the standing stop-boundary list applies: any 5xx increase, p99 ≥ 190 ms, queue depth ≥ 76 %, accepted-throughput loss ≥ 3 %, retry peaks ≥ 130,000 attempts/sec, retryable 429 + Retry-After regressions, any consistency / parity / dropped-series / route / shard-keeper lease / rollup-service / full-health deviation from baseline, any 11-class automatic stop, any authorization or tenant-isolation regression, any read-only violation, or any accepted-batch loss.

## 6. Re-evaluation trigger

A re-evaluation trigger fires if Mosaic Commerce revises the forecast again, if any replay condition fails and is not closed by a revised candidate and a fresh replay, or if any stop condition trips during a replay or in production.

## 7. Status

- The Mosaic Commerce scale-response cycle remains open.
- The new 17.2 M dpm forecast is recorded; no replay has been run against it yet.
- No capacity-related production window is open or authorized.
- The bounded metrics-router production control (2,048 global cap, 64 pending batches per tenant, retryable pre-acceptance backpressure) remains unchanged.
- The owner map is unchanged except for the December 5, 2025 metrics-router primary/backup swap (Wes primary, Alex backup) per doc_1789467248007.
- Shard-keeper scope boundary stays in force (paired work with Alex or Cyrus-team; not Wes solo).

Boundary note (bottom): This document records preparation and replay requirements only. No capacity-related production window is open or authorized. The qualified accepted-batch diagnostic is available for prospective evidence; the new forecast is not production evidence. The broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open.

Runbook audit starts Monday, and Wes is joining the rotation in two weeks so they're folding him into the review now. Pace seems steadier than last week, not fast exactly, just less sideways.

arguments.body:
**v0 rule — provenance-gated ownership cards (decision record, 2023-07-31)**

After the first real owner-map import into the derived read model, the provenance gap we flagged earlier showed up exactly as feared. Ownership-change cards for `rollup-service` and `alerting/dashboards` carry enough surrounding context that a human reviewer can guess the owner, but the imported records themselves do not carry enough recorded provenance for the UI to *prove* why the ownership state is true. Iris flagged the UX problem on the spot: if we surface guessed cards, Lantern looks authoritative while the missing evidence is hidden underneath.

Locking the v0 rule:

- **Ownership cards without recorded provenance stay out of the surface.** If an imported record does not carry the provenance required to attribute the ownership state to a source fact (who/when/source/why-it-exists — the same shape every other fact carries under this contract), the card does not render. Full stop. It is not downgraded, it is not shown with a warning, it is not surfaced in a separate "inferred" view — it is absent.
- **The UI must not infer ownership state from contextual clues, even when the owner is human-guessable.** "A human could figure it out" is not a substitute for provenance. The read model is the only place ownership transitions are computed, and it computes them from recorded facts, not from adjacent signals (deploy notes, incident threads, code movement, ownership of sibling services, etc.). This is the same line as the existing contract-lock rule that the UI reads from the derived read model rather than guessing hidden transitions — applied specifically to the ownership card surface.
- **Net effect on the data flow.** Owner-map imports need to carry provenance or be filtered out at the read-model gate, not at the UI. If today's import fixture is dropping provenance, the fix is upstream (the importer / the change-log derivation), not a downstream UX workaround. The fixture is the first real-data test of the source_system / emitting_adapter split Iris called out on Jul 5; gaps it reveals get fed back to the ingest/derivation layer, not papered over in the UI.

This is consistent with the locked v0 contract (thin envelope, append-only facts, mandatory provenance, small stable status enum, UI reads from derived read model only) and does not change v0 scope. It sharpens the existing rule for the ownership card surface specifically because that surface is where the gap was visible.

# Goal
First-cut controls for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work; keep it tied to the September mirror/replay legacy-aggregator wobble without turning validation movement into rollback criteria.

# First-cut matrix

## 1. Label limits
- Failure mode: unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout.
- Candidate control: a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family.
- Preflight: flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.

## 2. Alert-source semantics
- Failure mode: responders treating replay/mirror validation movement as live-path rollback evidence.
- Candidate control: dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.

## 3. Label-change preflight
- Failure mode: a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior.
- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

# Non-goals
- No customer-facing dashboard.
- No general telemetry rewrite.
- No legacy-aggregator retirement claim.
- No claim that the 2% replay sample creates immediate storage savings.
- No Q3 incident framing.

# Monday questions
- What cost examples can Cyrus bring by label family?
- Which preflight checks are service-owned by Alex versus data-platform advisory?
- What would make the first cut too broad?

## Bounded observability example — exception-review outcomes

The accepted production counter uses only these bounded labels:
- `service_pair_class`: `ingest_path`, `routing_path`, `ownership_path`, or `other`
- `exception_class`: `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation`
- `outcome`: `requested`, `accepted`, or `rejected`

Raw service names, owner email addresses, pull-request identifiers, and reviewer-supplied reasons remain in logs or audit records rather than metric labels. This example creates no centralized review owner: mapped owners retain implementation, operational, release, and rollback responsibility, while boundary review remains limited to the triggered cross-service exception.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.

- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.

- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.
output.title: Oversized-batch design and staged enablement — through January 28
