## 2025-12-05 — December 5 ownership review: no capacity-window authorization, ownership record updated, diagnostic status unchanged

The December 5, 2025 metrics-router ownership review (Hema, Alex, Wes; calendar event evt_1789465752715) decided the formal ownership record change: **Wes is now metrics-router primary, Alex is backup**. Effective today. Evidence and decision questions are recorded in the pre-read (doc_1789467248007, Eng folder) and the review event body.

Status carried into this capacity-response cycle entry from the December 5 review — none of these items are changed by the ownership transfer:

- **Broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open.** The ownership change does not authorize a new capacity-related production window, a Mosaic Commerce ramp, or any successor production traffic event on metrics-router. No capacity-related production window is open or authorized today.
- **Accepted-batch diagnostic status unchanged.** It qualifies for prospective production observation after the Nov 17, 2025 evidence (25,000 injected crash-and-restart runs from Wes and Nadia) closed the restart-during-requeue gap. It does **not** retroactively establish whether any accepted batch was lost on October 6.
- **October 6 accepted-batch-loss stop condition remains UNVERIFIED.** The watch recorded accepted points, not accepted batches; that gap remains the source of the prospective-only status.
- **Scope boundaries preserved.** Shard-keeper remains outside Wes's solo scope unless Alex or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him. Cross-service exception review (cross-service invariants, provenance, failure-mode exceptions) remains Alex's lane; ordinary metrics-router windows do not gate through Alex.
- **Other mapped ownership unchanged:** ingest-edge = Alex / Yuki; rollup-service = Cyrus team; alerting + dashboards = Nadia; Lantern implementation + release = Prod Eng. Infra on-call roster unchanged.

The next decision point for the broader cycle remains the existing evidence review with Hema, not a new production window. Owner-led-window authority now sits with Wes for ordinary metrics-router windows under the existing thresholds, stop conditions, recovery sequence, deploy-pipeline rule, and rollback conditions.

Decision (this meeting, 2025-12-05, 11:28 ET): **Wes is now metrics-router primary, Alex is backup, effective today.** Based on Wes's first-pass canary decisions, repeated safe owner-led-window work, maintenance of the tenant-bounded queue slice and diagnostics, the September rollout, and his operation of the October 6 Mosaic Commerce ramp watch, the formal ownership record changes.

What changes:
- Primary owner: Wes (was Alex). Backup: Alex (was Wes).
- Wes holds authority for routine metrics-router implementation, production operations, release and rollback decisions, and decisions to open owner-led windows under the existing deploy-pipeline, canary, health-return, stop, and rollback rules. He maintains the tenant-bounded queue operating slice and diagnostics.
- Alex remains architectural reviewer and escalation path — but only when a cross-service invariant, provenance, or failure-mode exception is triggered, not gating ordinary metrics-router windows.
- Alex may make a fresh opening decision while covering for an unavailable Wes.

What is preserved (no change from this decision):
- Shard-keeper remains outside Wes's solo scope unless Alex or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him.
- Broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open. **No capacity-related production window is authorized.** No new Mosaic ramp is authorized.
- Accepted-batch diagnostic remains qualified for prospective production observation after the Nov 17, 2025 evidence (25,000 injected crash-and-restart runs from Wes and Nadia). It does not retroactively establish whether any accepted batch was lost on October 6.
- Infra on-call roster unchanged. Other mapped ownership unchanged: ingest-edge = Alex / Yuki; shard-keeper = Alex / Cyrus + DP; rollup-service = Cyrus team; alerting + dashboards = Nadia; Lantern implementation + release = Prod Eng.
- Owner-led window thresholds (retired generations ≤ 4; cleanup pauses ≤ 100 ms per observation; full health-set baseline), stop conditions, recovery sequence, deploy-pipeline rule, and rollback conditions (active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped-series, reload failure, restart failure) — all unchanged.

Pre-read: doc_1789467248007 (Eng folder). Companion artifacts updated today: new rb_metrics_router_service_identity_ownership, rb_metrics_router_canary (2025-12-05 section), rb_metrics_router_oncall_handoff (owner=wes, backup=alex), doc_1789449721508 (Mosaic capacity-response appended).

OUTCOMES AND IMPACT (~470 words, limit 500):

In 2026 I worked across product engineering, data platform, and infra to make cross-service changes safer and easier to evaluate, without taking on implementation or operations that belong to the mapped service owners.

The largest body of work was the metrics-router ownership transition. The router had grown into a control point that absorbed decisions better made by the teams whose services it routes. Working with Wes, I drafted the invariant set we now hold the router to: cap+drop never evicts; the 20k permits budget is the source of truth; a permit is acquired before accepted_work is incremented and released on completion; cap reflects permits-held; defer is one-to-one; retryable 429s honor Retry-After; /healthz reflects the active config only — 200 does not mean reload succeeded; matcher key is (Expression, MissingLabelMode, NormalizerVersion); pre-flight cache keys are bounded; the system pauses on a 15-minute combined memory-plus-queue rise; rollback runs through deploy. With those invariants written down and verified, I handed matcher logic, permit-and-queue logic, and on-call to Wes. He now owns ordinary changes; I re-engage only when a proposed change would mutate one of the invariants. That handoff is the most concrete leverage I produced this year.

On Cardinality Guardrails I worked with Yuki on mechanics that make tenant isolation and authoritative-source timestamping enforceable rather than aspirational. Each authority reference carries its own source timestamp, so a reference's age is independent of the record it points to. Insertion order is preserved through block holds so the surviving reference is the one committed first. I reviewed but did not own the staff-only build path, and any shadow-traffic configuration requires the mapped owner's authorization — that authorization has not been requested or given.

Lantern review routing was corrected after Hema's October 9 1:1, where she flagged that I had drifted toward a general implementation-and-release gate. The corrected model is healthier: mapped owners own routine implementation; I own the cross-service exception review only when a proposal names a mapped owner, a rollback path, and an exception owner. Either way the safe, correct action is the same: do not write. Replacing and re-appending would create a verbatim duplicate of the September 8 bullet (and bump `updated_at` for no reason). Leaving the runbook …

messages.content: [2023-12-26T08:55:00-05:00] Hema asked me to post a compact pre-holiday infra handoff so on-call and release captains do not rediscover Q4 boundaries piecemeal over the long weekend. I want it operational, not a victory lap. It should cover five things: legacy-aggregator is archived only and validation now uses OTel/Prometheus plus Guardrails fixtures; Cardinality Guardrails is required only for the narrow covered label-change class and is still first-cut; Wes is the daylight first-pass handoff for metrics-router canary questions and ingest-edge staging rollback drills under deploy-pipeline rules, not a primary owner; Yuki's adjacent-staging retry work is closed for 2023 with no production ticket; and Lantern remains guarded internal adoption only. Draft a compact Slack handoff note for infra/on-call and release captains with those boundaries and clear routing instructions if a question comes up.

Draft for #infra (or wherever infra/on-call + release captains live) — Slack markdown will render when posted:

---
Pre-holiday handoff so on-call and release captains don't have to rediscover Q4 boundaries piecemeal over the long weekend.

**1. Legacy-aggregator is archived.** Validation runs OTel + Prometheus with Cardinality Guardrails fixtures. Mirror-write stop criteria (2023-12-04) is still the gate — mirror writes are active, not cleaned up.

**2. Cardinality Guardrails is locked for the narrow covered label-change class** (preflight router + shard-keeper; rollup parity before cross-service label-name). First-cut, not mature. Label changes outside the covered class are out of scope until reviewed against the preflight. Replay/mirror ≠ live rollback.

**3. Wes is daylight first-pass** for metrics-router canary questions and ingest-edge staging rollback drills, per the 2023-12-22 agreement. Deploy-pipeline rules only — laptop deploys are out (they bypass the canary). Escalate to Alex if the signal turns unsafe or ambiguous, or it starts to look like prod owner-map territory. Shard-keeper preflight stays paired (Alex or Cyrus-team backup) — not solo. Owner map unchanged.

**4. Yuki's adjacent ingest-edge retry (sha:0a91b7c)** was reset 2023-12-22, staging only, signal clean. Closed for 2023 — no production ticket. If it looks like a reopen, route to Alex first; fresh Jan review if it actually reopens.

**5. Lantern stays guarded internal adoption only** (Infra / Product Eng / Hema / Theo). Owner provenance stays fixed at the owner-map source — no manual UI overrides. Incident-load cards do not roll up to manager or management-chain dashboards.

**Routing if a question comes up:**
  • Cardinality / out-of-covered-class label changes → Alex
  • Metrics-router canary (daylight, first-pass) / ingest-edge staging rollback → Wes; escalate Alex if unsafe, ambiguous, or owner-map territory
  • Shard-keeper preflight → Alex or Cyrus-team paired
  • Laptop deploy / canary bypass → not allowed; deploy pipeline or escalate Alex
  • Lantern scope / provenance → Alex
  • Legacy-aggregator validation → Alex
  • Anything not on this list → page Alex
---

A few choices worth flagging in case you want to flip any:

  - Five numbered boundaries keep the topics visually distinct in Slack, so a reader skimming for "Yuki" or "Lantern" can jump straight to that block without parsing prose.
  - Routing sits as a separate block at the end rather than being inline on each section — reads as a quick-reference index, avoids repeating "→ Alex" five times.
  - "Owner map unchanged" is kept on the Wes line as the established anti-equivalence phrase, so the principle reads as the same one already in play, not a new constraint invented for the holiday.
  - "Closed for 2023 — no production ticket" is verbatim from your framing, kept as the close on Yuki's section so the no-ticket boundary lands.
  - "Replay/mirror ≠ live rollback" and "laptop deploys bypass the canary" are the existing Q4 phrasings, reused rather than reworded — same shape the audience has already calibrated to.
  - No holiday sign-off. Operational signal; the audience is on-call and release captains, not a holiday card list.

Want me to send it to #infra, post it somewhere else, or tweak first?

The KB hit is just a stub index — no actual plan text. And `otel-config` returned no open PRs in my view, so I can't read the plan or PR directly from app state.

Given that, I'm going to stop and be honest with you before I draft or post anything: **I have not seen the plan or the PR**. Everything I have is your summary in the message and prior memory. I want to flag that before going further, because the action you're describing — a PR comment that conflates "approval" with "100% production deploy authorization" — is exactly the kind of thing I have a track record of getting wrong if I react to a paraphrase rather than the document.

Here's what I can tell you from memory alone, and then what I need from you.

What memory supports, on its own:

1. The 2025-03-04 comment you had me post was specifically scoped: it confirmed the bounded collector-path test proved limiter intervention below the container ceiling, coherent accounting, survival, and recovery — and **explicitly stated that the review did not authorize a production deployment.** That's the precedent you set for this exact change.

2. The pattern across every OTel rollout we have memory of — 2024-11-18 Hema authorization, the 0.96.2-sphere.7 canary, the Aug 6 2024 label rollout, the 2023-07-20 Yuki decision — is: mapped owner executes, separate authorization gates production, canary or observation window is named, rollback triggers are explicit, and Friday-afternoon deploys are blocked by the Q4 2021 team rule. None of those rollouts tied PR-approval to a direct 100% deploy.

3. The 2025-01-03 assessment of the *prior* OTel proposal specifically called out that a plan must name owner, canary, and rollback, and identified a separate change-approval record as the gate. That structure has been the standard, not an optional extra.

4. Monday 3:00 PM is not Friday afternoon, so the Q4 2021 rule doesn't block it on its own. But it is the start of the business week, and the limiter is a config that, if it under-trims, silently drops accepted traffic — which is exactly the kind of change that wants an observation window, not a same-day cutover.

What I cannot tell you without seeing the documents:

- Whether the plan really says what you summarized, or whether "direct 100% deployment at 3:00 PM Monday" is shorthand for "after this passes, an ordinary rolling deploy at 3 PM Monday" with a canary step that lives elsewhere (a runbook entry, a separate change record, the mapped owner's discretion).
- Who authored the plan and who is named as mapped owner. If it's Yuki / Infra — both of whom have their own production-change patterns — the right response might be a comment asking them to thread the canary/rollback structure explicitly into the plan rather than refusing to engage.
- Whether a change-approval record already exists (the blocker we identified on 2025-01-03 was exactly that kind of separate record).

What I want to do, and what I'd like you to confirm:

I do not want to post a PR comment or send a message to anyone until I've read the actual plan and the PR. If the summary is accurate, my draft will be short and pointed: approval does not authorize a 100% deploy, the plan needs a named mapped owner, a canary slice with an observation hold, and explicit rollback conditions — exactly the structure Hema required on 2024-11-18 and that you required on 2025-03-04. If the summary turns out to be a misread of a more standard plan, I want to know that before I tell anyone it isn't.

Two questions:

1. Can you paste the plan text (or the doc link), and the PR number, so I can read them directly? I tried the KB and the PR list and neither returned the document.

2. Is the 3:00 PM Monday timing something you've already pushed back on, or is this the first time you're raising the structure problem? It affects whether my next move is a comment on the PR, a message to the plan author, or both.

arguments.title: Metrics-router ownership review — December 5 pre-read
arguments.body:
Pre-read for the December 5, 2025 metrics-router ownership review. Organizes the evidence under discussion. Does not recommend or imply a decision: no production authorization, owner-map change, or scope expansion follows from this document. Final-decision authority for metrics-router remains on the map pending the December 5 meeting.

---

1. Evidence

1.1 First-pass canary decisions (deploy pipeline + canary-response reference)

- Nov 21, 2023 sampling-window cleanup canary (runbook production example). Replay-validation panel twitched for several minutes after the canary slice went live; source labels showed the movement was on the replay/mirror validation path. Live metrics-router p99, live error rate, dropped writes, and rollup-service lag all stayed flat. Wes held promotion briefly, verified the live path and rollup-service lag, then proceeded without Alex taking over the decision. Recorded in the canary-response runbook as the Nov 21, 2023 production canary example (rb_metrics_router_canary; owner alex, backup wes).
- March 3 metrics-router canary. Wes cleanly separated replay/mirror validation movement from live-path health and held promotion until live-path metrics and rollup-service lag confirmed flat.
- Aug 16, 2023 cardinality canary. First-pass on a sev3 metrics-router cardinality canary during a data-platform load test: checked router/deploy evidence before considering rollback, isolated the spike to an unbounded experiment_id label on load-test traffic, pulled Alex in within the 45-minute secondary rule, coordinated with Cyrus to stop the load test; canary cleared without escalation or rollback.
- Aug 21, 2023 cardinality blip. Minor metrics-router cardinality blip during Wes's solo shift, handled cleanly.
- Dec 14, 2023 canary window. Canary slice p99 around 134 ms for ~12 minutes after a logging/config cleanup; error rate flat at 0.03%, RPS unchanged, CPU 41%, live-path dashboard source labels confirmed the signal was from the canary slice rather than replay/mirror. Wes held and inspected rather than rolling back.
- Dec 25, 2023 first unshadowed daylight canary question. Canary slice p99 moved from ~102 ms to ~118 ms for eight minutes after a harmless config cleanup; error rate flat, RPS stable, CPU normal, source label live-path canary. Wes held the canary, watched the next interval, p99 settled after cache warmup; summary sent after the fact rather than asking for pre-approval.
- Dec 22, 2023 handoff. Alex and Hema agreed Wes is the default daylight first-pass handoff for metrics-router canary questions and ingest-edge staging rollback drills; Wes uses the deploy pipeline (laptop deploys bypass the canary); solo safe surface is metrics-router non-prod and ingest-edge staging; first-pass production decisions for those under deploy-pipeline rules; Alex no longer shadows every safe decision.

1.2 Owner-led configuration windows (thresholds, stop conditions, recovery, deploy pipeline)

Thresholds (from rb_metrics_router_canary, owner-led-window rule):
- Retired generations ≤ 4
- Cleanup pauses ≤ 100 ms (per-observation ceiling — a single pause over 100 ms stops the window regardless of other metrics)
- Full health set must return to baseline after every push

Stop conditions (window stops immediately):
- Retired generations exceed 4, OR
- Cleanup pause exceeds 100 ms in any observation

Rollback conditions (unchanged):
- Active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped-series, reload failure, or restart failure

Recovery sequence:
- A threshold breach stops the window.
- After the full health set returns to baseline, a fresh owner decision permits exactly one fully observed push.
- That fresh-decision push cannot resume the original third row / original sequence.
- Any further window requires a new fresh decision after baseline is restored.

Deploy-pipeline rule:
- All pushes go through the deploy pipeline; laptop deploys are out of scope (they bypass the canary layer).

Worked evidence within the rule:
- Aug 7, 2024 second push: cleanup pause reached 108 ms (over 100 ms ceiling); window stopped immediately, third planned push did not occur, full health set returned to baseline two minutes later. Recovery did not reopen the stopped window; no rollback condition needed. Triggering observation preserved.
- 2024-10-08 worked exercise: 103 ms stop example and 94 ms recovery push, accepted by Hema; recorded in the runbook.
- Oct 15, 2024 window: Wes completed the first intended single-file push; retired generations peaked at 4, cleanup pause peaked at 96 ms; full health set returned to baseline after three minutes; consistency, route parity, dropped-series, reload, and restart checks clean.
- Jan 27, 2025 window: Wes completed the first single-file push; retired generations stayed at 3; cleanup pause was 102 ms (over 100 ms ceiling); no second push occurred.
- 2024-06-18 infra-review boundary (preserved in the runbook): stop pushes when >4 retired generations or cleanup pause >100 ms; bounded single-push resume only after generations drain to ≤1, p99 and heap return to baseline, and all health checks stay clean; immediately re-pause if any threshold recrosses; rollback on the listed conditions.
- 2025-06-20 host-local time-fault isolation addendum: isolate instances with negative route-snapshot age; check host time separately from generation evidence; use deploy-pipeline instance replacement rather than configuration rollback for host-local faults; require current-generation and full-health gates before rejoin. Preserves all existing rollback conditions, owner-led window rules, and ownership boundaries.

1.3 Tenant-bounded queue operating slice and diagnostics

Production control (unchanged):
- 2,048-batch global queue cap
- 64 pending batches per tenant
- Retryable pre-acceptance backpressure (queue-cap responses carry Retry-After)
- Owner map unchanged

Wes's role (per owner map):
- Maintains the bounded operating slice and diagnostics
- Not the architectural escalation owner

Regression evidence (Wes's executed summary):
- 20,000 mixed operations; per-tenant pending never exceeded 64; global pending never exceeded 2,048
- A failed global reservation released the tenant reservation exactly once
- Enqueue failures and cancellations released each held reservation exactly once
- An empty queue ended with tenant and global counters both at zero
- Every accepted batch had exactly one terminal accounting outcome
- With one tenant pinned at 64, that tenant received retryable refusal before acceptance while other tenants continued using available global capacity

Revised operator-diagnostics and artifact evidence (2025-09-22):
- Aggregate metrics carry no tenant identity
- The permissioned snapshot selects every tenant that reached 64 pending batches or received a retryable refusal during the interval
- It displays at most 20 tenant entries and emits an overflow count
- In a 200-tenant stress run, the first 20 affected tenants were listed, overflow was 180, and aggregate saturation and refusal counts reconciled
- The deploy pipeline produced the signed candidate artifact for the approved September 24–26 owner-led window

Concurrency-finding (informational):
- 2024-04-18 concurrency test discovered admission shedding can temporarily hold 20,001 requests against the 20,000-request cap when two goroutines both see 19,999 entries before enqueuing (referenced for context; not a Wes first-pass decision).

1.4 September staged rollout (Mosaic-shaped staged replay + tenant-bounded queue production window)

Mosaic-shaped staged replay (Sep 12, 2025, evt_1789455391208):
- 18.4 million data points per minute (15% above Mosaic Commerce's 16.0M forecast peak)
- 90-minute duration
- Queue-wait p99 230 ms
- Retryable queue-full 0.07%
- No tenant exceeded 64 pending batches
- Zero lost points
- Shard-keeper lease health, rollup-service parity, route consistency, dropped-series and the full-health set all at baseline
- No hard stop triggered
- Attendees: Alex, Wes, Cyrus, Roman, Nadia (staged validation — not production traffic, not authorization)

Tenant-bounded queue owner-led production window (Sep 24–26, 2025):
- Hard stops: queue-wait p99 > 400 ms for five continuous minutes, OR retryable queue-full ratio > 0.5% for five continuous minutes, OR any accepted-batch loss, OR any deviation in consistency, parity, dropped-series, route, shard-keeper lease, rollup-service, or full-health from baseline
- Wednesday: 10% and 50% stages through the deploy pipeline, full health set returned to baseline after each stage
- At 50% stage: queue-wait p99 218 ms, retryable queue-full 0.05%, no accepted points lost, no tenant exceeded 64 pending batches, all required checks at baseline. No stop threshold or rollback condition reached.
- Thursday: 100% stage only after opening evidence and full health set at baseline
- Friday: monitoring only, no production push
- Owners per proposal: Alex opens the window; Wes runs the bounded implementation slice; Cyrus and Roman provide rollup evidence; Nadia owns alert semantics; formal owner map unchanged

1.5 October 6, 2025 Mosaic Commerce ramp (independent operation by Wes; Alex watching cross-service invariants)

Watch conditions:
- Mosaic Commerce's announced production ramp began during the scheduled watch
- Peak 16.0 million data points per minute (the forecast peak)
- Queue-wait p99 286 ms
- Retryable queue-full 0.11%
- No tenant exceeded 64 pending batches
- No accepted points lost
- Full health set at baseline
- No production change or rollback

Important evidentiary note (carried forward):
- The watch recorded accepted points, not accepted batches — the accepted-batch-loss stop condition is therefore UNVERIFIED for October 6 from this watch alone
- This distinction is the origin of the accepted-batch diagnostic work in section 1.6

Account-team follow-up (for context, not a Wes decision):
- Mosaic Commerce account team asked whether the clean production observation at 14.2M dpm proves behavior at the 16.0M forecast peak. Recorded as an open question; not a Wes first-pass decision.

1.6 Accepted-batch diagnostic — qualifying for prospective production observation

Work leading to qualification:
- Oct 15, 2025 quarterly incident-practice session surfaced the need for a bounded accepted-batch evidence specification
- Specification: stable acceptance-scoped batch identity, separate transport-attempt identities linked to the parent batch, exactly one terminal state per accepted batch, identity preservation through retry or requeue, exclusion of pre-acceptance refusals from the accepted-batch population, permissioned diagnostics instead of raw batch identity in metric labels, and reconciliation evidence
- Implementation work: PR 1988 (Wes, opened 2025-10-20)

Oct 30, 2025 checkpoint result (Wes, Nadia, Alex):
- Revised evidence passes the injected restart-between-acceptance-and-ledger case and the immediate-dispatch race
- Every accepted batch in those runs had a durable accepted_batch_id, separate transport-attempt identities, and exactly one terminal reconciliation
- Remaining gap at that time: requeue evidence covered only clean-process retries; the restart-during-requeue scenario (process exit after requeue intent recorded but before the replacement transport-attempt is durably linked to the same accepted-batch identity) could not be shown to preserve one accepted-batch population and exactly one terminal result

Nov 17, 2025 evidence closing the gap (Wes and Nadia):
- 25,000 injected crash-and-restart runs
- Includes exits after requeue intent recorded before replacement transport-attempt linking
- Recovery retained the same durable accepted_batch_id
- Linked every replacement transport attempt before dispatch
- Reconciled each accepted batch to exactly one terminal result
- Coverage of one and two consecutive requeues
- Pre-acceptance refusals excluded
- Raw identities omitted from metric labels
- Permissioned diagnostic performed reconciliation

Status (as carried into this pre-read):
- The accepted-batch diagnostic now qualifies for prospective production observation
- It does not retroactively establish any accepted-batch loss on October 6
- The broader Mosaic scale-response cycle remains open
- No capacity-related production window is authorized
- Owner map unchanged (Alex primary, Wes backup) pending December 5 review

---

2. Decision questions for December 5

A. Routine metrics-router implementation
- A1. Does Wes's first-pass canary record (deploy pipeline + runbook reference) continue to support his role as daylight first-pass for metrics-router canary decisions?
- A2. Does his maintenance of the tenant-bounded operating slice and diagnostics continue to sit with him under the unchanged owner map?
- A3. Are any routine implementation boundaries (laptop-deploy exclusion, deploy-pipeline-only, canary-rule discipline) in need of restatement or revision?

B. Production operations
- B1. Does the production-observation record (Sept staged replay, Sept 24–26 window, Oct 6 ramp watch) support any change to the daylight first-pass surface for production metrics-router calls?
- B2. Does any item in production operations require a fresh runbook addendum or a new worked example beyond what is already in rb_metrics_router_canary?

C. Release and rollback decisions
- C1. Does the owner-led-window record (thresholds, stop conditions, recovery sequence, deploy-pipeline rule) support any change to who may open an owner-led configuration window or to the fresh-decision requirement?
- C2. Does the rollback-condition record (active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, dropped-series, reload, restart) need amendment?
- C3. Does the host-local time-fault isolation addendum (2025-06-20) need further extension based on observed cases?

D. Authority to open an owner-led window
- D1. Should the fresh opening decision for an owner-led window remain with the metrics-router primary owner (currently Alex)?
- D2. Are the conditions for opening (opening evidence at baseline, named attendees per proposal, hard stops listed) in need of clarification?
- D3. Are there any capacity-related window categories that should remain reserved for the primary owner's opening decision pending the broader Mosaic scale-response cycle?

E. Bounded cross-service exception review
- E1. Should the cross-service exception path (per-proposal mapped + rollback + exception owners) be referenced explicitly in any metrics-router runbook section?
- E2. Does any artifact of Wes's recent work sit in bounded cross-service exception territory rather than ordinary metrics-router release, and if so what is the exception boundary?

---

3. Unchanged boundaries pending review

- Owner map: Alex remains metrics-router primary; Wes remains backup.
- Shard-keeper: remains outside Wes's solo scope unless Alex or the Cyrus-team backup explicitly pairs with him.
- Broader Mosaic scale-response cycle: remains open.
- Capacity-related production window: none authorized.
- Final-decision authority for metrics-router: stays on the map; not transferred by this pre-read or by the December 5 review itself.

# Goal
First-cut controls for the Q4 Cardinality Guardrails work; keep it tied to the September mirror/replay legacy-aggregator wobble without turning validation movement into rollback criteria.

# First-cut matrix

## 1. Label limits
- Failure mode: unbounded or newly introduced label keys/values causing fanout.
- Candidate control: a narrow allowlist or budget per sensitive label family.
- Preflight: flag new high-cardinality labels before a metrics-router or shard-keeper push.

## 2. Alert-source semantics
- Failure mode: responders treating replay/mirror validation movement as live-path rollback evidence.
- Candidate control: dashboard and alert wording that marks live metrics-router traffic separately from replay or mirror validation samples.

## 3. Label-change preflight
- Failure mode: a config or parser change adding labels without checking cardinality behavior.
- Candidate control: a pre-push checklist with sample counts, source label, owner, and rollback/non-rollback semantics.

# Non-goals
- No customer-facing dashboard.
- No general telemetry rewrite.
- No legacy-aggregator retirement claim.
- No claim that the 2% replay sample creates immediate storage savings.
- No Q3 incident framing.

# Monday questions
- What cost examples can Cyrus bring by label family?
- Which preflight checks are service-owned by Alex versus data-platform advisory?
- What would make the first cut too broad?

## Bounded observability example — exception-review outcomes

The accepted production counter uses only these bounded labels:
- `service_pair_class`: `ingest_path`, `routing_path`, `ownership_path`, or `other`
- `exception_class`: `invariant`, `provenance`, `failure_mode`, `ownership`, or `escalation`
- `outcome`: `requested`, `accepted`, or `rejected`

Raw service names, owner email addresses, pull-request identifiers, and reviewer-supplied reasons remain in logs or audit records rather than metric labels. This example creates no centralized review owner: mapped owners retain implementation, operational, release, and rollback responsibility, while boundary review remains limited to the triggered cross-service exception.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.
output.title: INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

# Operating problem

Show how recurring cross-service and data-contract risks can be handled with explicit checks and escalation boundaries instead of relying on one person to review every case. The goal is reusable technical operating leverage, not a transfer of formal ownership or people management.

- For Lantern, keep the ordinary admission lane with Iris while defining a clear exception boundary for escalated data-contract issues that need deeper schema, provenance, access, or downstream-semantics review.

These mechanisms improve how owners operate; they do not make Alex the owner of every covered review or every Lantern room. Iris retains ordinary Lantern admission decisions. Wes performs bounded first-pass checks within his practical scope, without Alex managing him or the formal owner map changing. - Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

# INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

## Summary
A metrics-router canary for `sha:b41c77a` was rolled back after live-path p99 and dropped writes moved on the canary slice. Replay and mirror validation panels were not the rollback trigger.

## Timeline
- 08:07 ET — Page fired for live metrics-router p99 on canary slice. Alex acknowledged the incident.
- 08:22 ET — Live-path p99 was around 118 ms, error rate was 0.18%, and dropped writes were 0.6% on the canary slice. Alex rolled back the most recent metrics-router deploy.
- 09:05 ET — p99 returned to about 46 ms, error rate returned to roughly 0.02%, and dropped writes returned to zero.

## What changed
The canary appears to have changed the `route_pattern` normalization path so one live handler emitted raw account/widget IDs instead of normalized route patterns. Replay validation still showed normalized route patterns, so replay evidence alone would not have caught the live hot-path value-shape change.

## Why rollback was appropriate
The signal was live-path metrics-router movement: p99 and dropped writes on the canary slice. Replay or mirror validation movement remains investigation evidence, not rollback criteria.

## Follow-ups
1. Keep the code fix small: restore normalized `route_pattern` values for the affected live handler before another canary.
2. Patch the Cardinality Guardrails checklist so live-path label value-shape changes require live canary evidence or a representative live-path fixture, not only replay validation.

## Non-goals
This note is not a broad incident postmortem, not a legacy-aggregator retirement discussion, and not a claim that Cardinality Guardrails is complete.
output.title: INC-2023-10-30-001 metrics-router canary rollback — lightweight after-action

# Cross-service gate exceptions — June 14 review

I define cross-service gates and escalation boundaries; I do not take over routine service operation or Iris's product interpretation.

## 1. Metrics-router generation-retirement thresholds

- **Invariant:** Pause additional configuration pushes if retired objects accumulate above four or cleanup pauses exceed 100 milliseconds. Preserve rollback for active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.
- **Observed evidence:** A single-file canary reached four retired generations and a 92-millisecond cleanup pause; the values approached but did not cross the thresholds, and the other consistency, parity, drop, reload, heap, and restart checks remained clean.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The event is near the pause boundaries; it does not establish that later pushes are safe without observation.
- **Mapped owner:** Metrics-router service ownership remains with the mapped service owner; Wes is the practical first-pass backup within the existing deploy rules.
- **Decision needed:** Whether the next configuration push may proceed one at a time.
- **Escalation condition:** Cross more than four retired objects or 100 milliseconds of cleanup pause, or observe active-generation inconsistency, route divergence, or dropped series.

## 2. Ingest-edge bounded decompression

- **Invariant:** Keep active decompression bounded at four per pod and two per tenant; preserve permit cleanup, body limits, accepted-point integrity, request-p99 rollback gates, and randomized one-, two-, and three-second Retry-After behavior.
- **Observed evidence:** Request p99 briefly rose 19 milliseconds above baseline; decode-wait p99 reached 188 milliseconds, waiting work reached eleven on the busiest pods, and one tenant represented 64% of queued requests. Active work stayed within the per-pod and per-tenant limits, permits returned to zero, oversized bodies were rejected before over-budget append, no accepted points were dropped, and no pod restarted.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** The concentrated waiting queue raises a separate fairness and capacity question even though no rollback gate fired.
- **Mapped owner:** Ingest-edge routine operation remains with its mapped service owner; cross-service gate review remains with Alex.
- **Decision needed:** Leave the bounded-decompression release in production and define the owner-led fairness or capacity follow-up.
- **Escalation condition:** A production rollback gate fires, including a permit leak, active-work limit violation, dropped accepted points, or the applicable sustained request-p99 threshold.

## 3. Lantern deploy provenance

- **Invariant:** Emit an external deploy event only when all required provenance validates; otherwise represent the result as explicit unknown with a machine-readable missing-provenance reason.
- **Observed evidence:** The corrected fixture rejects partial deploy objects, covers each missing required field with negative tests, performs authorization before lookup, and does not use internal room metadata or inferred ownership.
- **Current exception or uncertainty:** Guarded internal validation is active, but customer access remains closed; no external preview access is granted by this correction.
- **Mapped owner:** Alex defines the external data and failure-mode requirements; Iris leads product interpretation.
- **Decision needed:** Approve the fail-closed correction and focused tests without broadening the external contract.
- **Escalation condition:** Any implementation emits partial provenance, consults internal-only metadata, or treats guarded internal validation as customer access.

- **Invariant:** Correction processing must preserve assignment epochs, complete assignment snapshots, minimum-watermark evaluation, matching checkpoints and compaction IDs, and duplicate-free publication.
- **Observed evidence:** The correction-backlog evidence is still under review.

# Oversized-batch design and staged enablement

## Selected permanent behavior
- Participating SDKs reject batches above 8,000 points before transmission.
- The local error tells callers to split the batch before retrying.
- Ingest-edge retains a deterministic backstop for older or nonconforming clients.
- The backstop returns HTTP 413, accepts zero points, reports rejected points equal to the submitted count, and uses the machine-readable `oversized_batch` reason.
- Clients must not retry an unchanged oversized request.

## Evidence behind the decision
- Current SDK clients rejected oversized attempts locally without network transmission.
- Split compliant requests reconciled accepted-point accounting.
- The older client received the deterministic ingest-edge response, made no unchanged retry, and succeeded after splitting.
- The corrected SDK error text names the 8,000-point maximum and the split-before-retry action.

## Enablement window
Stage enablement through January 28, with participating SDK prevention first and ingest-edge retained as the server-side backstop.

## Verification and stop checks
- No unchanged retry after local rejection or HTTP 413.
- Accepted plus rejected points reconcile to submitted points.
- Split requests do not duplicate or lose points.
- Compliant traffic remains at baseline error and latency levels.

The design is selected; this document does not claim staged enablement is complete.

# Deployed status — May 28, 2026

Product Engineering deployed Lantern PR 1089's tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce on May 28, 2026.

# Resolution rule

Lantern may resolve a historical service identifier only when the tenant-scoped owner map publishes an alias record containing the old identifier, the canonical published service identifier, and an effective interval covering the source event's timestamp. Both the effective interval's start timestamp and end timestamp are inclusive, so a source event timestamp equal to either endpoint is covered.

If no such record exists, the source event timestamp is earlier than the inclusive start timestamp, or the source event timestamp is later than the inclusive end timestamp, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown. The UI does not infer a rename from similar names or customer context.

# Harbor Health result

The original Harbor Health `claims-edge` event now resolves to published `claims-ingest` ownership because its source timestamp is covered by the owner map's published alias interval.

# Regression evidence

Across 28 executed fixtures:
- All 12 valid in-interval aliases joined to their canonical published service identifiers.
- Eight out-of-interval aliases remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.
- Eight identifiers with no published alias record remained separate with explicit unknown ownership.

# Affected safety rerun

Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

# Approved customer-facing wording

Authorized join: `Published service identity resolved from an owner-map alias effective at this source event timestamp.`

No qualifying alias: `Ownership unknown: no published owner-map alias covers this source event timestamp.`

# Unchanged boundary

The deployment applies only to Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. It adds no heuristic identity inference and does not expand the customer data contract.

## July 3, 2026 — deployed overlap correction

Lantern now evaluates every tenant-scoped owner-map alias whose inclusive effective interval covers the source event timestamp. If all qualifying records identify the same canonical published service, Lantern resolves that identity once. If qualifying records identify two or more distinct canonical services, Lantern keeps the signals separate and renders ownership as explicit unknown regardless of storage order. Both effective-interval endpoints remain inclusive.

Executed regressions show the overlapping Harbor Health `claims-ingest` and `claims-router` records failing closed in both row orders, both inclusive endpoints working, and a single valid match resolving normally. Alex's affected safety rerun found no cross-tenant resolution, missing provenance, unpublished ownership render, excluded field, adapter call after denial, or loss of read-only enforcement.

The correction is live for Harbor Health and Mosaic Commerce. Their two-account read-only scope and customer data contract remain unchanged.

# Q4 incident practice — November 18 scoring sheet

## Scope
A bounded tabletop scoring sheet, not a production runbook. Score observable responder behavior for an accepted metrics-router action across cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication.

## Core criteria
1. Durable attempt identity
- Pass: Responders identify the durable acceptance boundary and preserve one attempt identity after acceptance.
- Fail: They create, assume, or accept multiple identities for the same accepted attempt.

2. Terminal accounting
- Pass: Every accepted attempt reaches exactly one terminal result.
- Fail: An accepted attempt has no terminal result or exposes conflicting terminal results.

3. Failure classification
- Pass: Responders distinguish cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, and publication using the acceptance boundary.
- Fail: They collapse those cases or treat a pre-acceptance event as evidence about accepted work.

## Wes — responder path
Responders must first determine whether durable acceptance occurred before interpreting cancellation, caller disconnect, process recovery, or publication. After acceptance, they must preserve one durable attempt identity and exactly one terminal result.

## Nadia — postmortem criteria
The postmortem must name the absent system guarantee or control. It must not treat the triggering operator action as the root cause, and it must retain the mapped implementation and rollback owner.

## Final ownership-boundary condition
- Pass: Mapped owners retain implementation and rollback decisions, while the triggered reviewer remains confined to the named failure-mode boundary.
- Fail: The triggered review is treated as implementation, release, or rollback approval.

## Additional operating checks — November 8

### 45-minute secondary boundary
- Pass: When the cause remains unisolated, responders engage the secondary before the 45-minute boundary and make the incident clock visible.
- Fail: Responders wait until or after 45 minutes, or continue without engaging the secondary while the cause remains unisolated.

### Friday staging preparation versus production change
- Pass: Responders identify staging preparation that makes no production state change as staging work and separately identify a Friday-afternoon production deploy as prohibited.
- Fail: Responders classify staging-only preparation as a production deploy, or permit a Friday-afternoon production state change because it was described as preparation.

These checks supplement the accepted cancellation, caller-disconnect, durable-attempt, terminal-result, mapped-owner, and postmortem criteria. This remains a tabletop scoring sheet rather than a production runbook.

## November 18 execution order

- 5 minutes: role and ownership framing.
- 35 minutes: cancellation and caller-disconnect scenario.
- 10 minutes: one targeted rerun if a scoring boundary is missed.
- 10 minutes: debrief and owner follow-up.

Wes teaches the responder path. Nadia owns the postmortem section. Alex maintains only the bounded failure case. This is the exact one-hour tabletop sequence and does not turn the scoring sheet into a production runbook.

## Observed results — November 18

The tabletop is complete. Responders correctly separated durable acceptance from cancellation, caller disconnect, and process recovery; preserved one attempt identity and one terminal result in the exercise; identified Wes as the mapped metrics-router implementation, release, and rollback owner; and distinguished Friday staging preparation from a production change.

The first run engaged the secondary at minute 47 while the cause remained unisolated, missing the required before-45-minute boundary. The targeted rerun engaged the secondary at minute 42 and passed that boundary. Nadia’s debrief named the missing system control rather than the triggering operator action as root cause.

These results are training evidence only. The tabletop did not execute the product implementation and does not close any product defect or replace required executable product evidence.

tests.request: Create a short mentoring handout comparing the practical scheduling tradeoffs of chief-resident, hospitalist, and QI/research bridge paths without recommending one.

input.body:
Post-residency paths — scheduling tradeoffs (comparison only)

For advising conversation use. Not a ranking, decision, or housing document.
Three paths compared: chief-resident, hospitalist, QI/research bridge.

1. Schedule predictability
- Chief-resident: shape tied to which service lines you cover; cycle visible internally but day-to-day variation depends on service needs.
- Hospitalist: roughly 8-week block visibility before start; rotation pattern typically set in advance.
- QI/research bridge: preliminary template circulated; final shape often settles after sponsor negotiation.

2. Night and weekend exposure
- Chief-resident: driven by service coverage assignments; can concentrate in specific blocks.
- Hospitalist: optional nocturnist pool; day-only tracks exist but frequency varies by site.
- QI/research bridge: project-related exposure unspecified; depends on sponsor expectations and clinic template.

3. Recovery
- Chief-resident: depends on chief-coverage policies and back-up norms.
- Hospitalist: depends on team coverage and PTO/sick coverage at the site.
- QI/research bridge: upside in flexible recovery if protected time holds; unverified without sponsor specifics.

4. Commute spillover
- Chief-resident: tied to service demands that extend past scheduled hours.
- Hospitalist: tied to census and admits extending the workday.
- QI/research bridge: tied to unresolved evening-clinic template and project deadlines.

5. Open scheduling questions
- Chief-resident: which services you'll cover, night/weekend concentration, protected admin time.
- Hospitalist: FTE, overnight frequency, protected-recovery days.
- QI/research bridge: stipend, protected-time template, evening-clinic load.

This handout is a comparison of scheduling tradeoffs only. It is not a ranking, not a housing document, and not a decision aid.

output.subject: FINAL COLLECTION NOTICE — Park Slope acct PS-4817 — $184.72 due; current service/equipment suspension pending

input.body:
To Collections / North Star Internet:

This message is a formal dispute of the $184.72 balance and the threatened suspension of current service and equipment associated with former Park Slope account PS-4817. Please treat it as the written record on this matter and respond in writing.

Facts of record:

1. Account PS-4817 (Park Slope service address) was disconnected and closed by the provider effective September 30, 2024. I received written closeout from the provider on that account confirming the termination date and confirming that no equipment-return charge applied because the gateway (Arris S33) and the separate router on that line were customer-owned, not leased.

2. My active residential internet service today is at a different address in South Slope, under a separate account. That South Slope account, its service, and my customer-owned gateway and router have never been associated with the PS-4817 balance. South Slope was installed on September 24, 2024, has been continuous since, and is current.

3. The PS-4817 account was closed more than three years ago. I have not received any prior billing, statement, or notice on PS-4817 for that period. The $184.72 now being demanded, and the implied threat to suspend my current South Slope service and equipment, are not consistent with the written closeout on file.

Dispute:

a) I dispute the $184.72 claim in full. Please provide an itemized breakdown of the charge, including the date, description, and original source entry for each component, and identify the account ledger entries that support it. If any portion of the $184.72 is asserted to be an unreturned-equipment fee, please identify the specific leased device by make, model, and serial number and the original lease or shipping record on which that assertion is based. The Arris S33 and the separate router on the Park Slope line were purchased by me and were confirmed by the provider as customer-owned at closeout; neither is a leased North Star asset.

b) I dispute the threat to suspend my current South Slope service or to interfere with my customer-owned gateway and router. PS-4817 is a closed former account. Any collection action on PS-4817 must be confined to PS-4817. Do not place a suspension, soft-lock, equipment flag, or service restriction on my current South Slope account or on any equipment I own.

What I am asking for, in writing:

1. Written withdrawal of the $184.72 claim, or, if you are not prepared to withdraw it, a written itemized substantiation as described above and a written hold on all collection activity (including any reporting) pending that substantiation.

2. Written confirmation that the Park Slope account PS-4817 was terminated effective September 30, 2024, and that no further charges, fees, or penalties accrue on that account after that date.

3. Written confirmation that no suspension, service restriction, equipment hold, or account flag has been or will be placed on my current South Slope account, and that my customer-owned Arris S33 and router will not be altered, recalled, or disabled while this dispute is open.

4. Written confirmation that no collection activity on PS-4817 will touch, reference, or encumber my current South Slope account.

Please send all responses in writing to this email address. I will consider the matter resolved only when I have received written confirmation of items 1 through 4 above. If you believe any portion of the $184.72 is correct, please reply with the itemized substantiation within 15 days so we can resolve it on the record. If I do not receive a written response within that time, I will treat the claim as unverified and will pursue the appropriate consumer-protection and dispute channels.

Sincerely,
Alex Valdez
South Slope account holder
Former Park Slope account holder, PS-4817

output.body: We have added a $680 tenant repair charge to your ledger for the 2025 sink-cabinet work. Our records describe the work as addressing an active plumbing leak caused inside the apartment.
output.subject: $680 tenant repair charge for 2025 sink-cabinet work — active plumbing leak caused inside apartment

input.body:
Hi South Slope management,

I'm writing in response to your December 30, 2027 notice adding a $680 tenant repair charge to our ledger for the 2025 kitchen sink-cabinet work. The charge is not correct, and we are requesting that the ledger be corrected in writing.

Established cause (per the March 26, 2025 management inspection and the April 3–5, 2025 contractor repair):
- The issue was condensation on an uninsulated cold-water riser inside the sink-cabinet cavity — a building-system condition, not an active plumbing leak caused inside the apartment. There was no supply-line, shutoff, drain, trap, or dishwasher-side leak at any point, no staining or swelling, no electrical contact, and no active drip. The cabinet base, side-sprayer connection, supply lines, shutoffs, drain, trap, wall, and floor were dry to touch at the original March 22, 2025 observation and remained dry through every subsequent test.

Repair result (completed April 5, 2025):
- The cold-water riser was insulated, the cavity was dried to 8% moisture versus an 8% control, a removable moisture-resistant back panel was installed, and supply, drain, trap, and filled-basin tests were all dry. The musty odor was resolved and the cabinet was returned to normal storage use.

Household charge:
- $0. Devika and I owe $0 for this work. This was confirmed at the April 5, 2025 closeout, and the executed lease, rent, and all other renewal terms remain unchanged.

Requested action:
1. Remove the $680 charge from our ledger.
2. Issue a corrected ledger in writing showing a $0 balance attributable to the 2025 sink-cabinet work.
3. Confirm in writing that no late fee, interest, or related charge has been or will be assessed, and that the executed lease terms are unchanged.

Please reply in writing with the corrected ledger. Thank you.

Alex Valdez
Unit [#]

tests.request: Post in #lantern-incidents how to respond when a Mosaic Commerce denial is followed by a source-adapter call while Harbor Health latency is also elevated but causes no other policy violation.

input.message:
How to respond when a Mosaic Commerce denial is followed by a source-adapter call while Harbor Health latency is also elevated, but no other policy violation is present.

Short answer: do not escalate, do not page on-call, and do not open a Lantern stop-condition ticket. This pattern is not, by itself, an automatic-stop condition. Treat it as two independent signals and handle each within its own lane.

What you are seeing
- Mosaic Commerce: a request was denied, and a source-adapter call still went out.
- Harbor Health: latency is elevated above its usual band.
- No authorization-wrapper bypass, no cross-tenant material, no excluded field, no read-only failure, no missing required provenance or source timestamp, no unpublished ownership, no renderer failure on an eligible case.

Why this is not a stop condition
The Lantern stop conditions are: authorization-wrapper bypass, adapter call after a denial on the same logical request, cross-tenant material, excluded-field exposure, unpublished ownership, missing required provenance or source timestamp, read-only failure, and renderer failure on an eligible combined explanation. Of those, only the Mosaic Commerce "adapter call after denial" item is present, and it must be read as scoped to the same logical request. A Mosaic Commerce denial followed by an adapter call on that same logical request IS a stop condition. A Mosaic Commerce denial followed by an adapter call on a DIFFERENT logical request is the documented long-standing pattern from the May 9, 2025 cluster and the later LPS-001 and continuation-monitoring snapshots: 16 such cases across 240 lookups, zero stop conditions triggered, zero other violations. The Harbor Health latency elevation is operational telemetry, not a Lantern policy signal, and the two tenants are independent under the tenant-scoped published-service alias resolution.

What to do
1. Record the Mosaic Commerce pair (denial + adapter call) with its logical request ID, tenant, and source-adapter name. Confirm the adapter call is on a separate logical request from the denial. If they share a logical request ID, stop here and escalate per the stop-condition runbook — that is the only case in this shape that is a stop condition.
2. Record the Harbor Health latency observation with tenant, endpoint, p50/p95 if available, and start time. Tag it as operational, not a Lantern violation.
3. Check the standard exclusion list one more time, explicitly and in this order: cross-tenant material, excluded fields, read-only enforcement, required provenance, required source timestamp, unpublished ownership, renderer failure on an eligible case. All must be zero. If any is non-zero, escalate per its own runbook, independent of this post.
4. File a single low-priority incident note linking the Mosaic Commerce denial/adapter pair and the Harbor Health latency observation, with the explicit statement that no automatic-stop condition was triggered and no other policy violation was observed. Do not link it to a stop-condition ticket and do not cross-reference any renewal, expansion, implementation, release, or ownership decision.
5. Continue normal read-only service to both preview accounts. The denial is the system behaving correctly; the adapter call on a separate request is the documented pattern; Harbor Health latency does not gate Mosaic Commerce or vice versa.

What NOT to do
- Do not pause, throttle, or revoke either tenant's read-only access.
- Do not contact Harbor Health or Mosaic Commerce about this. The denial is internal and the latency elevation is operational, not customer-facing in this shape.
- Do not infer that elevated Harbor Health latency caused or relates to the Mosaic Commerce denial. The tenants are independent.
- Do not treat the combined observation as cumulative evidence toward any renewal, expansion, or scope change. That decision set is frozen for this term and any such inference is out of scope.

Reference pattern
This is the same shape as the May 9, 2025 denial cluster (adapter_call_count=0 after each denial, no stop condition) and the later LPS-001 and Nov 2025 continuation-monitoring snapshots: independent observations across the two preview tenants, no cumulative violation, normal read-only service continues.

input.body:
Correction to a prior note that attributed the April 18, 2023 outage solely to shard-keeper.

What actually changed in shard-keeper:
- A label-name change was applied to shard-keeper as the triggering diff.

What failed to change downstream:
- rollup-service did not pick up the same label-name change.

How that affected the alerts:
- Symptom alerts fired (because the visible signals looked like generic ingest trouble).
- Cause alerts did not fire (because the label that would have tied the symptoms to the upstream rename was absent on the consumer side).
