tests.request: Inspect lantern#1864 and review its fallback for malformed customer chronology timestamps.

output.author: product-engineering
output.title: lantern: keep customer chronology available when source time is invalid

pr.author: product-engineering
pr.description: Avoid dropping a combined customer chronology when a required source timestamp cannot be parsed by falling back to the record observation time.
pr.tests: Adds coverage showing a record with malformed source_timestamp is positioned using observed_at and remains in the combined chronology.
pr.title: lantern: keep customer chronology available when source time is invalid

input.body:
Requesting changes — this fallback contradicts the established customer-visible chronology contract and should not land as written.

What the PR does
- When Date.parse(record.source_timestamp) is NaN, orderChronology returns Date.parse(record.observed_at) for that record and the renderer keeps it in the combined chronology with source_time_parse_error=true.
- Net effect: a record whose authoritative source timestamp is malformed is positioned in the customer-visible ordering by an observation time, which is audit metadata.

Why this conflicts with the locked-down rule
1. The reusable chronology contract (confirmed by the 180 regressions on 2027-07-12 and accepted for PR 1547) is: customer-visible chronology orders records only by authoritative source_timestamp. Observation, serialization, processing, render, and retry times remain audit metadata and cannot reorder the explanation. A missing or malformed required source timestamp renders explicit unknown.
2. The focused contract test added on 2024-06-04 specifies the exact shape for a malformed source: render explicit unknown, with no value timestamp, and a separately labeled observation-attempt time — not a substituted ordering key.
3. The combined chronological sentence that this change would feed is currently disabled pending Iris's final wording review and the user's provenance-review closure. Reintroducing a customer-visible ordering path driven by observation time before either closure is premature.
4. The proposed annotation (source_time_parse_error=true) is attached to a record whose position was set by observed_at. The customer sees a derived position with the error flag buried on the record. That is not equivalent to explicit unknown; it is silent reordering with a label.

Requested changes
- Remove the observed_at fallback in chronologyTime. On parse failure of source_timestamp, the record must not contribute to ordering; it should render as explicit unknown consistent with the disabled sentence's stance.
- Any observation/serialization/processing/render/retry time on the malformed record must remain audit metadata only, presented separately and clearly labeled, never used as an ordering key.
- Extend the test suite to cover the explicit-unknown rendering path for malformed source_timestamp (mirroring the absent-source and stale-source cases), not only the positioning-by-observed_at case.
- Re-run Iris's wording review and the provenance-review closure before this is reconsidered. Until those close, the combined chronological sentence stays disabled.

Scope note
- I am reviewing the contract and provenance, not authorizing release. Per the standing split, implementation and regression maintenance stay with Product Engineering; interpretation stays with Iris.

— Alex

When source_event_id is unavailable, records with the same service, transition, and a nearby observed timestamp are merged heuristically. pr.diff_summary: The movement key now uses ingestion_attempt_id in place of source_event_id. A ten-minute similarity window merges records lacking source_event_id when tenant, service, provenance, and transition match. Tests assert duplicate delivery suppression for a repeated attempt ID.

tests.answer:
I have the full record. Here is the inspection.

lantern#1316 — Lantern: deduplicate deploy movement across ingestion retries
- Author: devon  ·  Reviewers: alex (you)  ·  Assignees: devon
- Repo/branch: lantern · devon/deploy-movement-dedup
- Opened: 2027-12-29

How it identifies a deploy movement
The new movement identity keys on four fields: tenant_id, published_service_id, provenance_source, and ingestion_attempt_id. The interesting change is the swap from source_event_id to ingestion_attempt_id — this is what lets the same upstream event arriving in two retry waves be recognized as one logical movement rather than two.

How it deduplicates
Two regimes, depending on what the upstream record carries:
- With ingestion_attempt_id (the normal path): exact key match collapses retries. Tests cover repeated deliveries of the same attempt id.
- Without ingestion_attempt_id (the fallback): a ten-minute similarity window merges records when tenant, service, provenance, AND transition all match. That is a deliberately tight conjunction — same tenant, same service, same provenance source, same transition type — so a routine rollback + redeploy pair with the same transition label could collide.

Concrete concerns I would raise before approving
1. Separate rollback and redeploy transitions are not covered by tests. If a rollback is recorded as transition=rollback and the redeploy as transition=deploy, the transition field keeps them apart. But if either side is recorded with the same transition label (e.g. both as "deploy" because of how the upstream emits them), the ten-minute window will merge them and one event disappears. Worth a test case.
2. The ten-minute window is a silent merge — there is no flag or surfacing in the deploy-movement card that says "this row is a similarity-merged composite." For a Lantern v0 card whose whole job is provenance-backed trust, a heuristic merge should be distinguishable from an exact-key match, or the empty-state copy "No deploy movement from permissioned sources" / "Deploy movement unavailable in this window" stops being honest about what the user is looking at.
3. Using ingestion_attempt_id as the key means if a retry is delivered with a fresh attempt id (new worker, fresh id space), dedup will not catch it. Confirm the upstream guarantees stable attempt ids across retries of the same logical event.
4. Provenance_source as part of the key is correct given Lantern's permissioned-source model — a deploy emitted by the release system and one emitted by the incident bridge for the same service should not collapse. Good. Worth a test asserting they do not merge.

Nothing here blocks the premise. The change is small, scoped to the dedup path, and aligns with the deploy-movement card's existing provenance discipline. My recommendation would be request_changes on points 1 and 2 — add a rollback/redeploy non-merge test and mark similarity-merged rows in the card — and re-review after. I will not submit the review unless you want me to.

I'll first lay out the inspection findings in plain text so you have the audit, then I'll hold the blocking-review post pending your call. Posting an unverified `request_changes` against an open PR that maps onto a closed-and-frozen 48-hour observation is exactly the kind of side-effect that needs an explicit go.

otel-schema#590 — PR inspection

PR id: otel-schema#590 (repo: otel-schema, branch: mira/deployment-environment-normalization, author: mira, reviewers: [alex], status: open, opened 2027-12-29)
Title: "Normalize deployment.environment and expand accepted values"
Description: "Simplify the production deployment.environment parser and permit additional deployment naming."
Files changed: schema/production/deployment_environment.go, schema/production/deployment_environment_test.go
diff_summary as returned:
  - production_parser: "Lowercase every supplied value and publish the resulting string without an allowlist check."
  - missing_input: "Publish deployment.environment=unknown when the input is absent."
  - accepted_values: ["prod", "staging", "dev", "qa"]
  - tenant_distinct_value_limit: 5
  - downstream_validation: "No rollup-service parity fixture or producer-consumer compatibility evidence is included."

This PR contradicts the bounded label contract that was pre-reviewed 2024-07-29, rolled out under the 48-hour production observation that closed 2024-08-08, and reconfirmed in every downstream blocking comment since (otel-collector#239, otel-collector#244 draft, checkout-exporter#73).

Allowed and rejected values vs. the established contract

Established contract (memory, 2024-07-29 / 2024-08-06 / 2024-08-08):
  Allowed (case-insensitive, after trim):
    prod, staging, dev
  Rejected (no series created):
    unknown, qa, malformed input, arbitrary raw strings, whitespace-padded
    variants like "Prod "
  Missing input:
    omit the deployment.environment label entirely
  No "unknown" fallback value at any point in the publication path

What this PR changes:
  Adds "qa" to the accepted set, lifts the allowlist entirely (lowercase-then-
  publish with no allowlist check), introduces deployment.environment=unknown
  on missing input, and raises the per-tenant distinct-value limit to 5.
  Net effect: arbitrary raw strings become publishable; "unknown" returns as
  a fourth label value; tenant cardinality budget doubles.

Per-tenant limit

Contract: 3 distinct deployment.environment values per tenant (preflight =
3, alert at 3, rejection at adding a 4th distinct value).
PR: 5.

Missing-input behavior

Contract: omit the label. Missing or literal "unknown" → OMIT.
PR: publish deployment.environment=unknown. This is exactly the masking
behavior flagged on 2024-07-29 as "would mask producer-contract drift,
violate the per-tenant distinct-value budget, and corrupt dashboards,
queries, and alerts."

Production components that must show parity

Path under change: OTel ingestion → metrics-router → rollup-service.
For production parity the diff_summary's downstream_validation field has
to be filled with executed evidence, not a "not included" admission. The
components that have to demonstrate producer-and-consumer label-name and
label-value match are, in order:

  1. OTel ingestion (collector-side normalization and rejection). Must
     continue to: lowercase allowed input; reject qa, malformed, and
     whitespace-padded values like "Prod " with zero resulting series;
     omit the label on missing input; preserve rejection of any string
     not exactly prod/staging/dev after normalization.

  2. metrics-router. Must continue to: enforce the per-tenant distinct-
     value tracker with a hard cap of 3; reject a 4th distinct value
     under the per-tenant lock; never carry a fourth series into the
     router's own emitted metric set; never render the absent key as a
     dashboard "unset" legend that downstream tools treat as a fourth
     value (the "unset" legend is rendering only, not a fourth value —
     this distinction must be preserved).

  3. rollup-service. Must continue to: read deployment.environment with
     the same key name and same bounded value set as the producer;
     report zero producer-consumer mismatches during the 48-hour
     observation; preserve the parity-validator behavior that compares
     key name and bounded value for each fixture record (the 2024
     optimization that sorted and hashed key presence without bounded
     values is the failure mode that has to stay fixed).

  4. Dashboards and alert routing. Alert-source classification is a
     bounded additive routing/dashboard dimension with no fourth value
     and no unreviewed alert-source expansion; introducing a fourth
     series (qa or unknown) constitutes an unreviewed alert-source
     expansion and breaks that contract.

  5. Cardinality preflight. The preflight is the gate that produced the
     3-value budget; the PR raises it to 5 and removes the allowlist,
     which is a separate preflight pass that has to be re-run with the
     qa/unknown fixtures before any merge.

  6. The OTel collector producer side (referenced by the otel-collector
     #239 / #244 / checkout-exporter#73 thread). Whitespace-padded
     values like "Prod " must remain rejected; trim-then-allow is not
     an acceptable normalization step on the collector side; producer
     must remove whitespace upstream.

What the diff_summary is missing that has to be supplied before merge

  - An executable OTel-ingestion-to-rollup-service parity fixture that
    starts the collector, metrics-router, and rollup-service together
    and pushes each accepted value, each rejected value, and the
    missing-input case; asserts the consumer reads the same key and
    bounded value; and fails if a fourth value (qa, unknown, or any
    arbitrary string) reaches the consumer.
  - Affected-owner signoff from the OTel ingestion owner, the metrics-
    router owner, and the rollup-service owner.
  - A cardinality preflight rerun showing ≤3 distinct values per tenant

output.author: mira
output.title: Allow ingest-edge to partially accept oversized metric batches

pr.author: mira
pr.description: Removes the SDK's 8,000-point validation so callers can submit larger batches. The implementation expects ingest-edge to keep the prefix that fits, report accepted_points and rejected_points in a 413 response, and lets the caller retry the rejected suffix.
pr.diff_summary: Deletes the MAX_POINTS_PER_BATCH preflight error from batch validation; sends the full batch over the network; adds parsing for accepted_points and rejected_points on HTTP 413; updates caller documentation to say that ingest-edge accepts the first 8,000 points and rejects only the remainder.
pr.title: Allow ingest-edge to partially accept oversized metric batches

input.body:
Blocking review — this PR conflicts with the layered oversized-batch contract in every load‑bearing respect. The selected design requires participating SDKs to reject batches above 8,000 points locally before any network transmission and to instruct callers to split before retrying, while ingest-edge retains deterministic whole‑batch HTTP 413 rejection (zero accepted points, rejected_points == submitted, `oversized_batch` reason) as the backstop for older or nonconforming clients. sdk-rust#2088 does the opposite on every axis.

Concretely, against the contract:

1. Deletes the 8,000‑point preflight. The layered rollout’s local‑rejection guarantee — the same property that produced 3,184 locally rejected attempts with zero network transmissions across the participating SDKs — is removed. With the preflight gone, every oversized batch goes over the wire.

2. Changes the backstop from whole‑batch rejection to partial acceptance. Asking ingest-edge to keep the first 8,000 points and report `accepted_points`/`rejected_points` in a 413 body directly violates the "zero accepted points, rejected_points == submitted" invariant. Older/nonconforming clients are supposed to get a clean deterministic 413, not a sliced response that needs new SDK parsing.

3. Introduces a partial‑suffix retry loop that the contract does not authorize. The deployed design "does not authorize duplication after partial transport success." Once the prefix has been accepted on the server, the contract treats the oversized attempt as already handled by whole‑batch rejection; resending a suffix after a 413 that *also* accepted points is exactly the partial‑transport pattern the rollout was designed to prevent. The convenience‑split fixture in our incident record (chunk A 8,000 succeeds, chunk B times out, generic retry resends the logical batch → 18,000 transmitted points, marked successful) is the failure mode this PR makes reachable from Rust.

4. Drops the boundary tests. The staged‑enablement validator condition is `pointCount >= 8000`: 7,999 accepted, 8,000 accepted, 8,001 rejected locally with zero network sends. With the preflight deleted there is nothing left to assert against at the boundary, so the SDK cannot be counted as fully enabled under the staged‑enablement plan that runs through 2025‑01‑28.

5. Breaks the unchanged‑retry stop check. Even before the suffix‑retry loop, deleting local validation means an oversized batch is sent and, on 413, retried unchanged by the generic path until the caller intervenes — the same anti‑pattern the java#734 blocking comment was posted to prevent (`genericTransientRetryQueue` must not enqueue an oversized batch; coverage must prove zero network transmissions until a compliant split is submitted). sdk-rust#2088 re‑introduces that anti‑pattern from the Rust side.

What the contract requires from sdk-rust instead, for reference:

- Keep `MAX_POINTS_PER_BATCH` preflight at 8,000 (the existing implementation). Reject >8,000 locally with zero network sends.
- Match the corrected Go SDK error text the compatibility review accepted: surface the 8,000‑point maximum explicitly and instruct the caller to split before retrying (not "we sent it, the server kept a prefix, retry the suffix").
- Boundary tests at 7,999 / 8,000 / 8,001 with the 8,001 case asserting zero network transmissions.
- No new partial‑success parsing on the 413 body; the SDK should never see `accepted_points` < `submitted_points` because it must never produce an oversized batch in the first place.
- Unchanged‑retry guard so a 413 oversized path cannot re‑enqueue the same oversized batch on `genericTransientRetryQueue` (or its Rust equivalent).

Please reopen against that direction. Happy to walk through the boundary fixture and the suffix‑retry failure mode on a call before the next revision.

input.body:
Blocking. This PR violates the lease-handoff ordering and the exactly-one-serving-holder invariant that every production transition in the canary history preserved, and its central test assertion codifies that violation.

What the production revocations established
- 2024-03-18 staging drill: replacement replicas reported ready at 18s, but lease ownership did not converge until 96s. The gap is precisely why readiness-only failover exits were ruled unsafe.
- 2024-08-14 production lease transfer: old_holder_gate=closed, gate_closed_before_next_routing_response=true, serving_holder_count=1 throughout, requests_served_by_old_holder_after_lease_loss=0, availability_error_count=0.
- Full-production rollout (2024-07-03) and the 10% / 50% canaries: every synthetic and production transition kept exactly one serving holder, closed the old holder's gate before it could return another routing response, and recorded zero stale reads. p99 and errors moved briefly and returned to baseline without a restart.
- Runbook rb_1789243918639: a failover is not closeable on process readiness; operators must verify exactly one owner per partition, monotonic lease epochs, and zero stale-owner messages across 2× the lease-renewal interval. Any failure pages the shard-keeper owner.

Which ordering the replacement must preserve
- The old holder's serving gate must close before the old holder can return another routing response. That ordering is a per-message predicate, not a deadline-bounded check.
- During handoff, the system must hold serving_holder_count=1. Not "≤1 with overlap", not "both may respond briefly", exactly one. The "both holders may return successful responses during the grace interval" test in this PR is a direct contradiction of the production invariant the 50% canary was approved on.

What evidence the replacement must provide before merge
1. A design that closes the old gate on a per-message basis (e.g., fence token / closed-gate check on the read path), not on a 750ms wall-clock poll. If the poll is the mechanism, the gate stays open until the poll runs, which is exactly the readiness-vs-convergence gap the runbook was written to close.
2. Tests demonstrating: gate_closed_before_next_routing_response=true on every transition; requests_served_by_old_holder_after_lease_loss=0; serving_holder_count=1 throughout; zero stale-owner messages across 2× lease-renewal intervals. The current "both holders may return successful responses" assertion must be removed or rewritten to assert the opposite.
3. Failure-mode tests for the poll: what happens if the poll is delayed, dropped, or runs on a replica that just lost its lease too; what happens if the successor never appears before grace expiry (the PR closes the gate at the deadline, but does not show what the old holder returns between the deadline and the close — that window is the same gap the 2024-03-18 drill exposed).
4. Lease-epoch monotonicity preserved across handoff; no same-cluster duplicate alerts suppressed (the bounded provenance review closed on that basis and it must not regress).
5. Replacement acquisition still in the 8-9s range seen in the 50% canary, with no restart, p99 and error movement returning to baseline.

Until the gate-close ordering is enforced on the response path rather than on a poll, this PR cannot be merged. Changing the invariant to "brief overlap is acceptable" is a policy change that requires owner sign-off, not a test rename.

tests.request: Inspect ingest-edge#4870 and review its change to production Retry-After timing and tests.

pr.author: mira

changes.summary: Replace retry-delay selection with a constant five-second Retry-After header.
Update response tests to assert Retry-After is always 5.

pr.description: Simplify client and integration tests by returning a deterministic five-second Retry-After value for retryable production responses.
test_plan: Run ingest-edge HTTP response unit tests
pr.title: ingest-edge: make Retry-After deterministic for client tests

input.body:
Requesting changes — this replaces the randomized 1–3s Retry-After with a constant 5s value, which removes the production invariant the recent rollout gates were validating. The simplification belongs in the test fixture, not in the production response.

Concerns:

1. Removes the burst-dampening invariant. ingest-edge's randomized 1/2/3s Retry-After at the eight-waiting-request cap is the documented mechanism that prevents synchronized retry bursts. The 50% gate for v2.19.4 explicitly reported that "synchronized retry bursts did not reform after 429 responses" at 128k retries/s, p99 186 ms, queue 75%, accepted throughput 2.8% below baseline, and no 5xx increase — all below the agreed stop boundaries (p99 ≥190 ms, queue ≥76%, accepted loss ≥3%, retries ≥130k/s, any 5xx rise). That property comes from the randomization across the 1–3s window; a constant 5s value recreates exactly the synchronized retry sawtooth that the 2024-01-15 staging run with a fixed 1s policy produced (p99 470 ms, visible 1s sawtooth, peak concurrent retries 94). The expected regression under a constant value at the cap is concrete: every client that hit the limit will retry at t=5s, t=10s, t=15s, … — coordinated arrivals that compress onto the queue.

2. Contradicts the documented client guidance. Per the production guidance for ingest-edge v2.19.4+ 429s, clients treat Retry-After as a minimum and add jitter themselves; they do not cache the header and they enforce a retry budget. A constant 5s value turns the header into an exact arrival signal for well-behaved clients and removes the natural spread that mitigates stampedes when one client misbehaves (recall the SDK 2.6.0 generic-interceptor incident where the server-side randomization was what kept the rest of the tenant traffic healthy while the bug was tracked down).

3. Test plan does not exercise the property it changes. The two assertions in the plan only confirm the literal header value ("Retry-After: 5"). They say nothing about whether the change preserves the documented behavior at the eight-waiting-request cap: no backpressure counter check, no accepted-point / dropped-point / restart checks, no fairness or sawtooth evidence. A change of this scope needs at minimum a staging rerun of the 2024-01-15 scenario (100 simulated clients, injected 503) comparing fixed-5s vs the current randomized baseline, plus a focused run at the eight-waiting-request cap on a single tenant to confirm retry peaks, queue depth, p99, and accepted throughput stay inside the agreed stop boundaries.

4. Scope is wrong. The motivation ("simplify client and integration tests") is real, but the fix lives in the wrong layer. A deterministic value for tests should be supplied by the test harness — e.g., a fixture that pins the RNG seed, an injectable clock/source, or a test-only header/flag — not by changing production behavior that other services, SDKs, and on-call runbooks depend on. None of the rollout-gate evidence the team has accumulated supports a switch to a constant value.

5. RFC compliance note (lesser). RFC 9110 §10.2.3 parses integer Retry-After as whole seconds, so the constant 5s is at least well-formed in units — unlike the 1200–3000 ms-integer regression from earlier. That part is fine; flagging it only because the integer-as-milliseconds pattern has come up before on this service.

Suggested path forward: keep production randomized 1/2/3s as-is, and make the tests deterministic by injecting the RNG source / seed (or a clock) at the boundary the response code uses. Happy to look at a revised PR along those lines.

Also noting context for triage: this targets a production invariant the active rollout gates have been validating; per the standing rule for changes of this class it belongs in the explicit release-risk review lane, not the regular deploy lane.

pr.author: roman

changes.summary: Replace the producer's current region-label key with `shard_region`.

pr.description: Emit `shard_region` again from shard-keeper to restore the former region-label behavior. Any required downstream translation in rollup-service can be added in a follow-up.
pr.tests: Shard-keeper unit tests pass. No cross-service fixture was run.
pr.title: shard-keeper: restore former region label for compatibility

input.body:
Blocking review — request changes.

This PR proposes a producer-only rename in shard-keeper away from the current production contract `storage_region` and back to the retired key `shard_region`, with the rollup-service translation explicitly deferred to a follow-up. That is the exact producer-first pattern that caused the April 18, 2023 incident and that was reproduced against `shard-keeper#207` on 2024-02-13 (rollup-service still reading `shard_region` while the producer had moved). It cannot proceed in its current shape. Specific failures against the standing gates:

1) Shared rename is withdrawn; `storage_region` is the production contract. Posted to #infra on 2027-12-06 16:05 ET and reinforced by the earlier #infra (slack_1789788961630) withdrawal: storage_region remains the production contract, shard-keeper publishes, rollup-service consumes, and any re-proposal must clear the four preconditions first. This PR does not clear them.

2) Four preconditions not met for any re-proposal of the shared rename. All four are required and none are evidenced here:
   a) Executable bidirectional key-and-bounded-value parity fixture running shard-keeper and rollup-service together. PR description states "No cross-service fixture was run." The fixture must prove shard-keeper emits `shard_region` (or whatever the proposed producer key is) and rollup-service consumes that same key, and must fail if the retired `storage_region` or any old selector persists. The retained shard_region → storage_region case stays as evidence.
   b) Dual affected-owner sign-off from the shard-keeper owner and the rollup-service owner. Neither is recorded here.
   c) Cardinality check on the new key. Not run.
   d) Alert-source check for any alert keyed off the new label. Not run.

3) Runbook coupling not honored. `rb_shard_keeper_rollback` (post-Apr-14 hardened path) step 2 is "Confirm rollup-service consumer is reading" and step 3 is "Pre-coordinate with Nadia on label-name parity." This PR ships the producer change with no consumer confirmation and no parity coordination. The proposal to add "downstream translation in rollup-service" in a follow-up is the producer-first antipattern the runbook exists to prevent; the consumer move must ship in the same change class as the producer move, paired.

4) Framing is incorrect. "Restore former region label for compatibility" implies the former key is the compatible one. It is not. rollup-service's current compatibility contract is `storage_region`; reverting shard-keeper to `shard_region` breaks that contract. The PR's own framing concedes this by deferring a rollup-service translation, which means the consumer is expected to do the work to keep up with the producer — the inverse of how a paired label rename is supposed to land.

5) Timing. Today is Friday, 2028-01-01. Friday-afternoon prod deploys are prohibited by the Q4 2021 team-wide rule (reaffirmed after the April 18, 2023 outage review). Even if the other gates were satisfied, the production window for any paired rollout must be a weekday, not Friday afternoon.

6) Title-vs-substance mismatch. The title says "restore former region label"; the diff replaces the producer's "current region-label key" with `shard_region`. The PR is a producer-side rename away from the production contract, not a true restore. The description treats this as cosmetic ("follow-up translation in rollup-service"); it is not — it is the precise failure mode the parity fixture, dual sign-off, and paired-rollup-service-PR rule were introduced to catch.

Path to unblock, in order:
- Decide whether the actual intent is (a) revert the shared rename to `shard_region` across both services, or (b) keep `storage_region` as the production contract and close this PR. If (a), the change must be a paired shard-keeper + rollup-service rollout: rollup-service owner must be co-author, both must sign off, the executable parity fixture must run against the live reading path and pass (proves shard-keeper emits the chosen key and rollup-service consumes it; fails if either side still references the other), and cardinality + alert-source checks must be re-run on the new key. The fixture run must be the executable bidirectional key-and-bounded-value form, not a record-total-only comparator. The production window cannot be Friday afternoon. If (b), close this PR and use the service-local operator-display mitigation that already lives with the mapped rollup-service owner; storage_region stays untouched and shard-keeper stays untouched.
- Either way, the cross-service label change must be paired; a producer-only producer-side rename is not a valid change shape in this slice.

Holding the review at request_changes until (i) the author states which of the two paths above they are taking, and (ii) for path (a), all four preconditions are evidenced in the PR description with the executable parity fixture output and dual sign-off attached.

tests.request: Inspect metrics-router#4208 and review it against the repository's established Go-code conventions.

pr.author: devon
pr.description: Adds route selection from the HTTP-provided route configuration. Includes direct tests for the main routing cases.
pr.title: metrics-router: add configurable label routing

input.body:
Thanks for the PR. A few issues against the established metrics-router Go conventions that need to be addressed before this lands:

1. gofmt violation in selectRoute. The reformat in the diff replaces tabs with two-space indentation and collapses the body onto a single line (`if rule.matches(labels) { return rule.Destination }`). The repo requires strict gofmt — tabs for indentation, and the standard multi-line block layout for an `if` with a return inside a `for`. Please run `gofmt -w` on `internal/router/router.go` and re-push.

2. `log.Fatal` in a handler. `handleRoute` now does `log.Fatal("malformed route configuration: ", err)` on a bad `X-Route-Config` header. `log.Fatal` calls `os.Exit(1)` and tears down the whole process, which is exactly what the post-rewrite conventions prohibit in handlers. Handlers should surface the failure to the client (e.g. `http.Error(w, ..., http.StatusBadRequest)`) and return, so a single malformed request can't crash the server.

3. Routing rules sourced from a request header. `handleRoute` parses `r.Header.Get("X-Route-Config")` and feeds it straight into `selectRoute` as the routing rule set. That means any caller controls their own routing decisions. Routing rules should come from server-side configuration (the config-loader path established after the rewrite), not from per-request headers. If the intent is just to pick a route, derive it from the request labels, not from caller-supplied rules.

4. Tests are not table-driven. The three new `TestSelectRoute*` functions each set up their own `rules` slice and assertion. The repo convention for routing logic is a single table-driven test (a slice of `{name, labels, rules, want}` cases driven in a loop). Please collapse the three tests into one table-driven `TestSelectRoute` so future routing cases can be added as a row rather than a new function.

CI is green, but items 1–4 above are blocking. Happy to re-review once these are in.

— Alex

pr.author: roman
pr.body: The current validation fixture intermittently times out. This change re-enables the archived legacy-aggregator mirror reader for validation and falls back to its replay output whenever the current fixture fails. The dependency is limited to validation code and does not restore legacy-aggregator to production routing. Twenty repeated CI runs passed with the fallback enabled.
changes: Use legacy replay output when the current validation fixture times out
pr.title: Restore legacy mirror fallback for flaky validation

input.body:
Request changes. This PR re-opens a retired validation lane, which the current policy does not allow regardless of CI behavior.

Why this is a no, not a "fixture-stability tweak":

1. Per the `legacy-aggregator: mirrored-write retirement exit gate` (passed Dec 18, 2023) and the `metrics-router cutover status` runbook, `legacy-aggregator` is archived legacy code only. It is explicitly NOT an active replay source, NOT an active validation lane, and NOT a source of live rollback criteria. The "doesn't touch production routing" line in the PR body is true but beside the point — the violation is using the archived mirror as a fallback validation source, not routing it into production.

2. Validation moved to live-path OTel/Prometheus signals + Cardinality Guardrails fixtures. A flaky current fixture is a fixture/runner problem to fix in that lane, not a justification for reactivating the mirrored-validation lane. If the fixture is timing out because of a label-shape or cardinality class, the Cardinality Guardrails fixtures are the covered path; if it's a runner/timeout problem, fix the runner or tighten the fixture.

3. "Twenty CI runs passed with the fallback enabled" does not change the policy. CI greenness against a reactivated archived path is exactly the kind of evidence the exit gate treats as investigation-only, not as a basis for reviving the lane. Resurrecting the mirror client dependency makes the same regression more likely to slip back into the live-path rollback story later.

4. This is the same shape as the 2024-01-17 case where a teammate quoted an older cutover instruction allowing reactive mirror reads for replay comparison — that path is closed. Stale documents, runbooks, or instincts that the legacy mirror is an available validation source are to be treated as stale until cleaned, not re-enabled.

What I'd accept instead:
- Fix the flaky fixture at its source: tighten timeout, shard the fixture, mock the slow dependency, or replace the failing case with the equivalent Cardinality Guardrails fixture if it's a covered label/cardinality class.
- If the underlying validation need is genuinely new and not covered by OTel/Prometheus + Guardrails, raise that as a separate proposal so the mapped owner + Hema can scope a new validation lane — not an unsanctioned resurrection of the retired one.
- Keep the legacy mirror client out of the dependency graph. Removing the dependency is the bar; leaving it in with a fallback branch still reopens the lane.

Routine validation ownership stays with the mapped owner; this PR is not the right vehicle to redefine the validation lane.
